title: Why Team India player was penalised after Women's Asia Cup final
description: India pacer Kranti Gaud admitted the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by Supriya Rani Das of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees. As a result, there was no need for a formal hearing.
fullText:
NEW DELHI: India pacer Kranti Gaud has been fined 10 per cent of her match fee for breaching the ICC Code of Conduct during the Women's Asia Cup final against Sri Lanka in Dubai on Sunday.

Gaud was found guilty of a Level 1 breach of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel.

Gaud breached Article 2.5 of the ICC Code of Conduct, which relates to "using language, actions or gestures which disparage, or which could provoke an aggressive reaction from a batter upon his/her dismissal during an International Match."

The incident took place in the first over of Sri Lanka's innings. After dismissing opener Imesha Dulani, Gaud gestured in the direction of the pavilion.

Gaud admitted the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by Supriya Rani Das of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees. As a result, there was no need for a formal hearing.

On-field umpires Saleema Imtiaz and Shathira Jakir Jesy, third umpire Rokeya Sultana and fourth umpire Humaira Farah levelled the charge.

Along with the 10 per cent fine, one demerit point has been added to Gaud's disciplinary record.

It was her first offence in a 24-month period.

Level 1 breaches carry a minimum penalty of an official reprimand and a maximum penalty of 50 per cent of a player's match fee. They can also result in one or two demerit points.

Pakistan have been fined five per cent of their match fee for maintaining a slow over-rate during their Women's Asia Cup semifinal against Sri Lanka on Friday.

G.S. Lakshmi of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees imposed the sanction after Pakistan were found to be one over short of the target after time allowances were taken into consideration.

Under Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which deals with minimum over-rate offences, players are fined five per cent of their match fee for every over their team fails to bowl in the allotted time.

Pakistan captain Fatima Sana pleaded guilty to the offence and accepted the proposed sanction. Therefore, there was no need for a formal hearing.

On-field umpires Vrinda Rathi and Shathira Jakir Jesy, third umpire Rokeya Sultana and fourth umpire Rabab Ahsan levelled the charge.

title: Maldini driving licence suspended after car crash
description: Italy international Daniel Maldini has his driving licence suspended following a car crash in Milan.
fullText:
Italy international Daniel Maldini has had his driving licence suspended after he was found to be over the legal alcohol limit following a car crash in Milan.

Maldini, son of Italy and AC Milan legend Paolo and grandson of the similarly feted Cesare, was one among six people to suffer minor injuries after his Porsche Carrera 4 collided with another vehicle in the early hours of Sunday.

The attacking midfielder had scored the winning goal for Cagliari in a 2-1 win against his parent club Atalanta in Serie A just hours before the accident.

Milan city police confirmed to BBC Sport that there had been a road traffic accident involving the 24-year-old footballer.

It said: "Mr Maldini was administered a breathalyser test at the scene" and his "driving license was confiscated following a positive result".

He was taken to hospital for precautionary checks before being released.

According to reports, an initial breath test carried out by the police at the scene of the accident recorded a blood alcohol level of 0.91 grams per litre, while a second reading registered 0.89 g/l - both higher than Italy's legal limit of 0.5 g/l.

In a statement, Cagliari said Maldini had "undergone toxicological screening following recent media reports" and that "all tests returned negative results".

The club added Maldini will join the squad for training on Monday to prepare for the team's forthcoming fixtures.

Maldini became became the third generation of his family to play for Italy when he made his debut against Israel in a Nations League fixture in 2024.

He has made six appearances for his country, with the latest coming in September 2025.

title: Davey reignites international ambitions with Wales
description: Uncapped Wales scrum-half Megan Davey's admits she almost called it quits before her recent call-up at the age of 26.
fullText:
Megan Davey's international ambitions have been reignited at her self-proclaimed 'old' age of 26.

Loughborough Lightning's record appearance holder considered going into full-time teaching when she did not make Wales' 2026 Six Nations squad.

Her hopes were dashed again when omitted from Sean Lynn's extended training squad for the WXV Global Series.

"There was a little bit of a wobble," admitted uncapped Davey.

"It's hard to keep going when you're at my age, you feel old in the game."

But the half-back received a call-up last month and is now part of the 39-strong squad which will take on South Africa, USA and Japan.

"There's always been something inside me, I know I can do it, it's the voice inside my head that's kept me going," she said.

"I was really happy that I got an opportunity."

Rose out of Wales WXV squad with injury

Davey qualifies for Wales through her grandfather from Llanelli but went through the English pathway system as a youngster.

"The avenue for under-20s was always really with England because it wasn't as set up with Wales, but now it's really good," she said.

"I'm a little bit older... now I feel like I can really do people proud."

And despite being a latecomer in camp, Davey says everyone has been welcoming.

"There's always that thing when you walk into an environment that's already established, you're like 'how am I going to do?' but I was really raring to go," she added.

"Obviously a bit sad that I wasn't in the squad to begin with, but you just crack on with what you're doing."

Live on BBC One, iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage

Davey has primarily trained at scrum-half with Wales and faces competition from Keira Bevan and Seren Lockwood.

And contrary to the stereotype of the position, the nines get along with no animosity.

"We all really enjoy each other's company. We want each other to do well, so there's never that hatred towards each other," said Davey, who has previously started at fly-half for Loughborough.

"Whoever goes out there and does the job first is the best pick for the team and you just need to back that completely."

Wales open their WXV campaign against South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park on Friday, 18 September (19:15 BST), and any potential involvement would mean the world to Davey.

"Playing international rugby is such a privilege and I want to make everyone proud - my family, but also the coaches that have been behind me for the last 15 years of my journey," she said.

"It's just that final step, like 'I made it'. I'm really excited and hopefully it comes at some point."

title: Benn unsure on future after defeat by Garcia
description: Conor Benn says he does not know what is next in his career after a crushing world title defeat by Ryan Garcia.
fullText:
Conor Benn says he does not know what is next in his career after a crushing world title defeat by Ryan Garcia.

The Briton was stopped in the second round on Saturday - only the second loss of his 10-year professional career - as American Garcia retained his WBC welterweight crown in Las Vegas.

Benn, 29, was fighting at welterweight for the first time in more than four years and had said the fight would be his last in the division.

"Everybody keeps asking 'what's next for Conor Benn? The truth is, I don't have the answer," he wrote on Instagram., external

"I've always wanted to be a servant of the public and give everything I have when it matters.

"But giving everything comes at a cost. And the people who have paid that cost more than anyone are my family and my kids.

"They've sacrificed time with their dad so I could chase this dream. They've had to share me with this sport their entire lives.

"So when people ask me what's next for Conor Benn, right now the answer is simple. Time with my kids."

Garcia reality check bursts Benn's bubble in Vegas

Benn, the WBC's number one contender, was outclassed by Garcia, who was making his first defence of the title.

Benn was taken to hospital after the fight, in what was understood to be a precautionary measure.

He turned professional with limited amateur experience, bypassed the traditional British, Commonwealth and European title path and built much of his reputation fighting against ageing former champions.

Benn said he planned to move up in weight regardless of Saturday's result.

The two defining nights of his career came at middleweight against Chris Eubank Jr, and a trilogy bout with Eubank remains a possible route back into the spotlight.

title: Ahead of Fed meeting, Trump says US should have world's lowest interest rate
description: DOONBEG, Ireland, Sept 13 (Reuters) - No country should have lower interest rates than the U., President Donald Trump said on Sunday, days before the Federal Reserve's ‌next policy meeting.
fullText:
DOONBEG, Ireland, Sept 13 (Reuters) - No country should have lower interest rates than the U.S., President Donald Trump said on Sunday, days before the Federal Reserve's ‌next policy meeting.

Speaking to reporters at the Irish Open golf tournament, Trump said he did not know ‌whether Fed policymakers will raise interest rates at their meeting this week. But he said the U.S. "should be paying the lowest interest rate in the ​world" no matter what the Federal Reserve's data indicates about inflation and the economy.

The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index, a key measure of underlying inflation, on Friday posted its largest increase in four months. That reinforced expectations that the U.S. central bank will raise the target range for its federal funds rate, now at 3.5% to 3.75%, at the conclusion of ‌its Federal Open Market Committee meeting on ⁠Wednesday.

Price pressures remain elevated as the economy deals with Trump's import tax increases and surging energy prices tied to the Iran war. Many at the Fed worry that the longer ⁠inflation remains high, the greater the cost will be to get it back to target.

The central bank's governors are meeting just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans keep their slim majorities in both chambers of the U.S. Congress. A rate ​hike ​could add to voter concerns about affordability, according to recent Reuters/Ipsos polls.

Trump's ​approval ratings have fallen as inflation has persisted. ‌He has argued that the Fed's interest rate levels have helped other countries at the expense of the U.S.

"I know more about formulas than anybody, and with the best credit in the world, we make other countries rich," Trump said on Sunday.

The president, a frequent critic of former Fed Chair Jay Powell, has been more supportive of Fed leadership since his own pick for chair, Kevin Warsh, took charge earlier this year. But Trump recently has made his ‌demands more clear.

"LOWER THE RATE OR I'LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES ​WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT," Trump posted on social media two ​weeks ago.

In additional remarks to reporters later on ​Sunday before he boarded a plane to return to the U.S., Trump reiterated that threat and ‌said: "We don't want to have deficits with nations. We ​want to have surpluses or ​at least break-evens."

Trump "will defend the independence of Kevin Warsh above all" no matter what the Fed does with interest rates, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told "Fox News Sunday."

But Hassett also underscored Trump's own preferences, saying that ​if the Fed raises rates, "I'm sure ‌he's not going to be super happy about it."

title: From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed
description: Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.
fullText:
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.

Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.

The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.

Playing on through injury could have had dire consequences for the rest of her season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try to play in the final Grand Slam of the year.

"I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said.

"We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great.

"I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain.

"I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."

Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week, but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.

She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.

Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding.

"I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said.

'Tough to control emotions' as Sabalenka suffers another near-miss

Rybakina wins US Open to inflict further pain on Sabalenka

Listen: US Open podcast - Rybakina crowned champion

Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.

Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.

She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.

Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but it was Rybakina who dominated the decider.

While her Belarusian opponent grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed.

"The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."

However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.

At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she coolly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.

The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.

Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.

On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.

She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride".

"I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said.

"There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table.

"It's not going to be easy to hang on to it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."

Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.

After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.

She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1,000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.

Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times.

"I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."

title: Dominant Kerr wins $150k with GB's first Ultimate title
description: Josh Kerr ends a sensational season by winning the Ultimate Championship 1500m title as the inaugural edition of athletics' new global event concludes.
fullText:
Josh Kerr ended a sensational season by being crowned Britain's first winner at the Ultimate Championship with a dominant 1500m victory - and earning $150,000 - as the inaugural edition of athletics' new global event concluded in Budapest.

Kerr smashed the 27-year mile world record at the London Diamond League and won Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow this summer, after beginning an outstanding year by reclaiming the world indoor 3,000m title.

In the shape of his life, Kerr swept past American Yared Nuguse on the back straight in Hungary and would not be denied once he had made his move to the front, taking victory in three minutes 29.35 seconds.

"I am a major championship guy and I will always say that," Kerr, 28, told BBC Sport.

"From seven weeks ago in London, I went home, I chopped wood and carried water and I was ready to go again.

"Sometimes you have to come out of it to dig deeper and go further in life. Two weeks before [a race] I try to do something to get me out my routine and then I push myself for the last few weeks. If I didn't finish with a win, then that was on me."

The 2023 world champion did not qualify by right for the Ultimate Championship, which is reserved for reigning global champions, Diamond League winners and others based on world ranking.

He was instead awarded an exceptional invitation by World Athletics, alongside rival Jakob Ingebrigtsen - although the pair's eagerly-anticipated reunion did not transpire after the Norwegian withdrew following his 5,000m win on Friday.

Kerr was peerless as he seized the opportunity to put on one final show this season - and take his share of the biggest prize pot in the sport's history.

Over the past three nights, the world's top athletes competed for a new title and a total prize fund of $10m (£7.4m) at the innovative event, which World Athletics president Lord Coe hopes can play a key role in shaping the sport's future.

title: World championship leader Antonelli wins Spanish GP
description: Kimi Antonelli extended his lead in the world championship with his eighth victory of the season at the Spanish Formula One Grand Prix at the Madring on Sunday.Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, who had scored points in every race this season, missed out completely, retiring his Ferrari on lap seven because of brake failure.
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli extended his lead in the world championship with his eighth victory of the season at the Spanish Formula One Grand Prix at the Madring on Sunday.

The 20-year-old Mercedes driver finished clear of Max Verstappen (Red Bull) and Lando Norris (McLaren) and is now 81 points ahead of nearest rival, his Mercedes teammate George Russell, in the title race.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) finished fourth ahead of fellow Briton Russell and Liam Lawson in the second Red Bull.

Franco Colapinto (Alpine), Oscar Piastri (McLaren), Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) and Niko Hulkenberg (Audi) rounded out the top 10.

Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, who had scored points in every race this season, missed out completely, retiring his Ferrari on lap seven because of brake failure.

George Russell was another big loser, with the Mercedes driver suffering badly from his team's decision to put him on two-stop strategy - the only one of the main runners to have this - which blew his chances of podium and left him even further behind his teammate in the title race.

Norris will also rue his team's poor strategy.

The reigning world champion drove a blistering lap on Saturday to claim pole position and was leading comfortably until the intervention of the virtual safety car (VSC) on lap 15.

While Antonelli and Verstappen immediately dived into the pits to change their tyres McLaren kept Norris out for an extra lap.

As he prepared to come in, the VSC finished meaning he lost time against his rivals, and the Briton wasn't helped by a slow pitstop of seven seconds.

He clawed his way past Russell and moved into third when Leclerc finally boxed on lap 48 of the 57, at which point the lead was handed to Antonelli who cruised home to take the chequered flag.

title: The tournament Jannik Sinner is aiming to return at is revealed in new injury update after missing the US Open
description: The 2026 US Open unfolded without the world’s best tennis player, Jannik Sinner, in action. Sinner, who was denied in last year’s final at Flushing...
fullText:
The 2026 US Open unfolded without the world's best tennis player, Jannik Sinner, in action.

Sinner, who was denied in last year's final at Flushing Meadows by Carlos Alcaraz, has been sidelined since his Wimbledon triumph with a knee injury.

The setback saw the world number one withdraw from the Canadian Open, the Cincinnati Open and ultimately the US Open.

In Sinner's absence, his rival Alcaraz made his long-awaited return to tennis after four months out and reached the quarterfinals in New York before being beaten by Ben Shelton.

With Alcaraz officially back and healthy again, it won't be long before Sinner makes his comeback to the ATP Tour.

According to Sky Sports Italy, Sinner underwent a three-week course of treatment at J Medical in Turin for extra-articular tendon inflammation.

Everything reportedly went well, and Sinner is now due to head back to his main residence in Monte-Carlo.

Sinner is set to resume training and is looking to finally return to professional tennis at the China Open in Beijing, which starts on the 30th of September.

He is the defending champion at the ATP 500 event, having comfortably beaten Learner Tien in the final last year.

Sinner also captured the China Open title in 2023 and finished as the runner-up in 2024 after delivering a thrilling final against eventual champion Alcaraz.

Sinner will not be taking part in the Laver Cup in London, which gets underway on the 25th of September.

Both Alcaraz and Sinner's time out has presented a golden opportunity for several stars to do well at big tournaments.

Taylor Fritz was the first player to take advantage of their absence, with the US number two clinching the Washington Open title at the start of the North American hard-court swing.

His compatriot, Shelton, then followed suit at the Canadian Open, where he defended the title to win his second ATP Masters 1000 crown.

The Cincinnati Open was won by 22-year-old Arthur Fils, who put together an impressive run to hoist his first Masters trophy.

The US Open will mark the second Grand Slam this year not won by Sinner or Alcaraz, with Shelton and Alexander Zverev set to battle it out for the title.

The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party rattled European politics this week after a convincing victory in a German state election, which placed it only a few seats away from forming the country’s first state-level far right government since the second world war.

“Gut gemacht!” Musk posted on X a week ago, using the German phrase for “well done” as he congratulated AfD party leader, Alice Weidel. It was one of at least a dozen posts the Tesla and SpaceX CEO made about the AfD following the result.

The AfD reciprocated Musk’s praise, with the party’s Saxony-Anhalt leader, Ulrich Siegmund, thanking the tech mogul for his support. Siegmund, who wants German schools to focus less on responsibility for the second world war and whose top staffers include four former members of a banned neo-Nazi youth group, called Musk a “visionary”.

Musk has become a central figure in the global far-right in recent years, using his support and influence to back anti-immigrant activists, illiberal leaders and nativist parties. Along with a preoccupation with race in the UK, much of that attention has been focused on the AfD, and the major results in the Saxony-Anhalt election, and Musk’s jubilation at their win, have revived scrutiny of his connections to it.

Musk’s ties to the AfD and German far-right predate the Saxony-Anhalt vote and coincide with the billionaire’s own public rightward drift. His views on immigration, politics and race, which he expresses relentlessly on X, have over the years become indistinguishable from many AfD policies. In boosting the AfD and receiving their adulation in return, Musk and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US.

As Musk became more involved in politics in 2024, backing Donald Trump’s reelection with over $100m of his own money, he formed alliances with several other international far-right leaders who hold anti-immigration views and antipathy for democratic institutions.

Musk has appeared onstage with Argentina’s chainsaw-wielding Javier Milei, presented an award to Italy’s ultraconservative prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, then attacked Italian judges ruling on migrant rights and gave a livestreamed speech at UK anti-Islam activist Tommy Robinson’s rally where Musk claimed immigration was causing “the destruction of Britain”.

Musk also connected with Naomi Seibt, a German climate crisis skeptic and anti-immigration activist who frequently posts on X and was 24 years old at the time. Musk began personally messaging her after seeing her posts, Seibt told reporter Paul Ronzheimer of Axel Springer’s Global Reporters Network, and she promoted the AfD to him in their chats.

In late 2024, Musk wrote an opinion column for the German outlet Die Welt expressing his own support for the AfD. Musk’s op-ed claimed that Germany was on the brink of “economic and cultural collapse” that could only be solved by the AfD, which he called “the last spark of hope” for the country. He also argued that the party wasn’t extreme, giving the example that its leader Weidel has a same-sex partner who is from Sri Lanka.

“Does that sound like Hitler to you?” Musk wrote.

As Musk took a prominent role in the second Trump administration at the beginning of 2025, he used his platform and newfound political power to further boost the AfD. In early January of that year, Musk hosted a livestream for Weidel that researchers found gave her a huge boost on the platform as well as translated to a jump in German-language media coverage.

“Musk did in fact have an agenda-setting effect on traditional media in Germany,” said Jan Rau, a researcher at Research Institute Social Cohesion and Leibniz-Institute for Media Research. “You could very clearly see it. There was a huge spike of attention from traditional media for Weidel in that moment, and a lot of this attention was actually connected with Musk.”

Weeks after hosting the livestream with Weidel, Musk also appeared via livestream at an AfD rally. Only days after causing an uproar for delivering fascist-style salutes at a Trump inauguration rally, Musk told the AfD crowd in Germany that there was “too much focus on past guilt, and we need to move beyond that”. His remarks drew condemnations from Jewish leaders and accusations that he was attempting to normalize the far-right.

Musk’s close proximity to Trump and prominent role in the White House following the 2024 election magnified his political power, as well as fears from foreign governments that he was interfering in their national affairs.

After acquiring Twitter in 2022, Musk made several changes that helped boost the divisive, far-right politics of parties like the AfD. He reinstated previously banned far-right accounts, such as pro-AfD, anti-immigration Austrian activist Martin Sellner – who has taken credit for mainstreaming nativist “remigration” policies – and often promoted international right wing accounts through reposts.

“The changes Musk made to the platform has made it much easier for far-right communication,” Rau said. “That’s helpful for the AfD in many ways.”

But researchers including Rau also argue that the rightwing bubble Musk has created on X has its limits. Only around 5% of Germans use X to find news, according to a 2026 Reuters Institute survey, and many mainstream figures in the country have publicly given up on using the platform. While some of Musk’s backing of the AfD crossed over to mainstream attention, much of it in recent months has been confined to his captive audience on X.

Today, Musk is deeply unpopular in Germany, with a YouGov poll last year finding that only 19% of the country had a favorable view of the multibillionaire. Fewer still, only 13%, viewed his attempts to influence German politics acceptable. Even within the AfD, Musk is not an entirely welcome presence.

“Musk’s boosting, in some quarters, is not particularly helpful,” said Oliver Marsh, an independent researcher formerly at the nonprofit Algorithm Watch. “A lot of the party are traditional German nationalists and don’t really approve of an American billionaire weighing in on German politics”.

While the AfD’s ascendance has more to do with Germany’s domestic politics and social dynamics than it does with Musk, it did not stop him from taking some credit for their success. Musk reposted a claim from a Germany rightwing media commentator that the tech billionaire’s ownership of X had caused a “vibe shift” that led to the AfD’s victory.

In the days after the AfD’s election success in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, Musk both celebrated the result and tried to claim that the party was not far-right at all but ideologically moderate. Musk posted that the party, which Germany’s own domestic intelligence agency last year labeled a rightwing extremist group, should be considered “far center”.

Musk also sought to reject American news media’s descriptions of the AfD being far-right, despite the party’s well-documented and extreme views on issues such as immigration, Islam and LGBTQ+ rights. Musk posted multiple replies to the Wall Street Journal and CBS News following the state election, attacking the outlets for using “far right” in their coverage.

“You are lying by calling AfD ‘far-right’,” Musk responded to a CBS News post on X, adding in another post that “‘far right’ is a propaganda term”.

The AfD party platform includes bans on public displays of Islamic beliefs; opposes same-sex marriage and adoption, despite Weidel’s long-term domestic partnership with a woman, which includes children; emphasizes ethnic-German identity and calls for mass deportations. AfD leaders also have received criticism over the years for downplaying the Holocaust and making provocative references to Nazism, with one of the party’s top members convicted in 2024 of using a Nazi paramilitary wing slogan during a rally.

Weidel has meanwhile claimed there is “a holy war against the German population” while calling for “remigration”, a term for mass expulsions once popular in far-right and white nationalist circles that has now been embraced by nativist parties as well as Musk and Donald Trump.

Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the AfD’s win this week by warning that the party’s true goals amounted to ethnic cleansing, a characterization which the far-right party denounced.

“If what is being advocated here, namely ‘remigration’, were to become reality, ⁠it would be nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” Merz said.

Musk once again defended the AfD, reposting a user criticising Merz’s allegation to his more than 241m followers.

Musk’s views, which include a fixation on race and vocal opposition to immigration, have come to closely resemble those of Weidel and the AfD.

“Anyone who opposes remigration is a traitor,” he posted in July.

description: Great Britain's Georgia Taylor-Brown wins the women's event of the World Triathlon Championship Series in the Czech Republic.
fullText:
Great Britain's Georgia Taylor-Brown produced a dominant display to win the final women's event of the regular World Championship Triathlon Series (WCTS) in the Czech Republic.

The 32-year-old finished the punishing hilly course at Karlovy Vary 36 seconds in front of the United States' Taylor Spivey, finishing the 1.5km swim, 40km bike ride and 10km run in two hours three minutes five seconds.

Germany's reigning champion Lisa Tertsch came third, one minute 28 seconds behind Taylor-Brown.

It was the Briton's best performance of the WCTS season and first victory on the tour since 2023.

She has concentrated on longer distances this season, with the 2020 Olympic silver medallist winning on the T100 tour in Spain in May - her best previous result in the WCTS this season was fourth in Samarkand in April.

Compatriot Beth Potter, who went into the event in second place in the overall standings, finished down in sixth, almost two-and-a-half minutes back.

Of the other British competitors, Kate Waugh was 10th, Sian Rainsley 14th and Olivia Mathias failed to finish.

Sunday's results meant that Potter was unable to capitalise on the absence of WCTS leader Cassandra Beaugrand of France, who chose not to compete.

Beaugrand leads the championship with a maximum 4,000 points going into the WCTS Grand Finals in Pontevedra, Spain, on 26 September.

Olympic champion Alex Yee heads the British challenge in the men's event on Sunday in Karlovy Vary, which is due to start at 14:00 BST.

title: 'Tough to control emotions' as Sabalenka suffers another near miss
description: After losing another Grand Slam final, Aryna Sabalenka smashes her racquet in frustration at a year that has seen her lose her world number one status.
fullText:
Aryna Sabalenka cut a forlorn figure as she sat staring into space following a painful defeat by Elena Rybakina in the US Open final.

As Rybakina celebrated her third Grand Slam title following a 6-4 5-7 6-2 win in New York, cameras pictured Sabalenka deep in thought as she sat in silence with her team.

At a tournament which has delivered so much success for two-time champion Sabalenka, the disappointment the 28-year-old has faced in the past week leaves her with plenty to ponder.

Not only has Rybakina replaced Sabalenka as the world number one after 99 weeks at the summit, she has now ended the Belarusian's 20-match winning streak at Flushing Meadows.

Defeat also means Sabalenka will end the year without winning a Grand Slam title for the first time since 2022.

For four-time Grand Slam singles champion Sabalenka, the disappointment was palpable.

Throughout the final, faced with a composed Rybakina who put together an outstanding performance, Sabalenka could not keep her frustrations at bay.

Her racquet felt the brunt of her exasperation as she slammed it to the ground after offering a break point to Rybakina in the second set.

After Rybakina sent an ace past her to secure victory, Sabalenka flung her racquet away in disgust before congratulating her opponent. As Rybakina waved to the crowd, Sabalenka sat on her chair and smashed another racquet against the floor.

Sabalenka also used an expletive as she told a cameraperson to go away as she sat with her team immediately after defeat.

"It's really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat," Sabalenka said afterwards.

"So I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn't be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there.

"So I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside."

Rybakina wins US Open to inflict further pain on Sabalenka

From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed

Sabalenka is always vocal on court and has been known to berate herself and roll her eyes ironically when missing points, even in her most dominant of victories.

Often she can channel her emotions into her aggressive hitting, but former British number one Annabel Croft believes it contributed to her downfall against Rybakina.

"It was extraordinary to witness because she had been very negative on herself with her body language in that first set and suddenly the emotions got the better of her," Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I felt like that really contributed to her going down in that first set. She was beating herself."

Sabalenka held back tears during a post-match interview in which she praised Rybakina's performance.

Croft says the Belarusian would benefit from applying the same level of poise during her matches.

"I think what happened was the minute she started to not respect the level of tennis her opponent was playing, she couldn't handle it at all," said Croft.

"You have to respect what they're putting out there and applaud it but then find ways to dig in and find another way to compete with them.

"It was almost like throwing the toys out of the pram today."

The weight of expectation Sabalenka puts on herself has affected her in major finals in particular.

She has won four of her nine Grand Slam singles finals, and only won one of her four finals as the world number one.

All five of her major final losses were in three sets, and on two of those occasions Sabalenka won the opening set.

After defending her US Open crown in 2025, she began this year targeting more Grand Slam success.

However, she lost a tight three-set Australian Open final to Rybakina before she imploded at the French Open. Leading Russia's Diana Shnaider by a set and 4-1 in the quarter-finals, Sabalenka totally lost her way, being dragged into a decider that she lost 6-0.

At Wimbledon, Sabalenka lost in the fourth round to Japanese four-time Grand Slam winner Naomi Osaka in what was her earliest Grand Slam exit for four years.

Sabalenka has won three WTA titles this year, triumphing in Brisbane, Indian Wells and the Miami Open, but she has been second best to Rybakina in the hard-court majors.

The US Open was meant to salvage Sabalenka's season - but she must now regroup as she adjusts to her position as world number two.

"I think overall I should be happy with the level I played, and there's lots of things to take from this tournament," Sabalenka said.

"Experience shows that I only come back stronger and all of these lessons this season definitely already made me stronger, but definitely going to motivate me for the next year to do a better job."

title: World Athletics' stance on Russian athletes 'won't change' - Coe
description: Sebastian Coe says that World Athletics' stance on sanctions imposed on Russian athletes "will not change".
fullText:
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe says the governing body's stance on sanctions imposed on Russia will not change.

Athletes from Russia and Belarus have been banned from international track and field competition by World Athletics since the country's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The Russian Athletics Federation has filed a new claim with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to challenge the sanctions imposed by World Athletics.

But Coe said: "Our position hasn't changed. This isn't about politics or passports, it's about the integrity of competition."

Russian Athletics says the ongoing sanctions "infringe on the organisation's rights", adding they "prevent it from fully representing the interests of Russian athletes on an international level".

Should the Cas ruling come down in favour of Russian Athletics, the way could be opened for Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete at the next Olympic Games, which will be held in Los Angeles in 2028.

Coe, who won two Olympic gold medals during a celebrated athletics career, has pledged to attend the Cas hearing to help present the case of World Athletics.

Speaking on Sunday at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, the 69-year-old Briton said: "From the age of 18, I believe that every position I've taken, whether it was during the creation of the first IOC athletes' commission or positions I've personally taken, it's about integrity and it's about competition.

"That matters to me, so our position won't change."

Coe added that the issue needed to be "resolved" and that the overall objective was to have a "full complement of people on a global level competing in our sport".

Russian Athletics executive director Boris Yaryshevsky, in an interview with the Russian TASS news agency last week, criticised Coe's intention to attend the Cas hearing.

"It is very clear that he has something personal," said Yaryshevsky.

"He is no longer speaking on behalf of World Athletics as a federation. He is speaking for himself, saying that he personally will go to court to defend this.

"I believe this is simply his personal position, not the position of World Athletics."

The stance taken by World Athletics differs to that taken by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), as well as the governing bodies of numerous other sports.

The IOC provisionally lifted Russia's suspension in July, potentially allowing the country to compete at the 2028 Olympics Games in Los Angeles.

Other sporting federations, including World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing, have this year removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing.

Some Russian and Belarusian athletes competed as neutrals at both the 2024 Paris Games and this year's Winter Olympics in Milan.

title: US Open champ Rybakina on top of world after injury scare
description: Elena Rybakina is on top of the tennis world, celebrating her first US Open title and her rise to number one barely more than three weeks after she feared injury would force her out of the final Grand Slam of the year.Kazakhstan's Rybakina beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday to claim her third Grand Slam title.
fullText:
Elena Rybakina is on top of the tennis world, celebrating her first US Open title and her rise to number one barely more than three weeks after she feared injury would force her out of the final Grand Slam of the year.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday to claim her third Grand Slam title.

She'd already assured herself of toppling Sabalenka from the number one spot just by reaching the semi-finals.

"I can't find words right now, honestly," Rybakina said. "I don't expect nothing like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with a little bit with an injury, but somehow everything aligned together on my side."

The "little bit of an injury" saw Rybakina hobble out of her Cincinnati quarter-final on August 20 -- 10 days before the start of the US Open -- unable to put weight on her left heel.

"It wasn't the best time, for sure, because I was so upset," Rybakina said. "I didn't know actually how it's going to be day by day.

"We arrive to New York. We did MRI. It didn't look that great. We had to talk with a lot of doctors to get opinion what we should do."

With a doctor in Australia providing valuable long-distance advice, Rybakina and her team came up with a plan to manage her training, rest and treatment and give her a chance at her second major title of the year, after her victory over Sabalenka at the Australian Open.

Her run to the final included an impressive fourth-round victory over two-time champion Naomi Osaka before come-from-behind wins over resurgent Olympic gold medallist Zheng Qinwen and former champion Coco Gauff.

It all led to her 18th showdown with Sabalenka in a rivalry that has emerged as the most dynamic on the WTA tour.

Having narrowed Sabalenka's lead in their head to 10-8, Rybakina is looking forward to more chances to take on her fiery rival, whose on-court personality is the perfect foil to her own cool approach.

"I don't know what the future will bring, but it's always very difficult matches against Aryna," she said. "I feel like we push each other to be better after such tough battles."

The two seem destined to tussle for the top spot for some time. But other players -- Gauff and Jessica Pegula -- also had a chance to seize the number one ranking in New York, so Rybakina knows that Sabalenka is not the only rival she must be wary of.

"I feel like not only with her, with also other players, top players, you always want to try something new, to change in your game, to be better," she said.

"I don't know what future is going to bring, but I hope success and some more wins."

title: From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed
description: Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.
fullText:
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.

Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.

The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.

Playing on through injury could have disastrous consequences for the rest of the season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try and play in the final Grand Slam of the year.

"I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said.

"We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great.

"I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain.

"I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."

Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.

She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.

Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding.

"I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said.

Listen: US Open podcast - Rybakina crowned champion

American Shelton to face Zverev in US Open final

Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.

Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.

She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.

Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but Rybakina who dominated the decider.

While the Belarusian grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed.

"The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."

However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.

At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she cooly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.

The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.

Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.

On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.

She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride".

"I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said.

"There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table.

"It's not going to be easy to hang onto it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."

Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.

After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.

She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.

Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times.

"I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."

title: Rybakina wins US Open to inflict further pain on Sabalenka
description: Elena Rybakina demonstrates why she is the best women's player in the world by beating Aryna Sabalenka to win her first US Open title.
fullText:
Elena Rybakina demonstrated why she is the best women's player in the world by beating two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka to win her first US Open title.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina already knew she would be the new world number one after Saturday's final regardless of the result, and she celebrated with a 6-4 5-7 6-2 victory over the player she will replace.

Rybakina was the more composed of the two throughout as she claimed the third Grand Slam title of her career, having triumphed at Wimbledon in 2022 and the Australian Open earlier this year.

Sabalenka hoped to soften the blow of losing the top ranking by winning a third consecutive US Open title - but looked fraught in a tense performance.

Rybakina and Sabalenka have developed a strong rivalry built not only on their outstanding talent but their contrasting personalities.

And Rybakina's ice-cool composure - the direct opposite of the Belarusian's combustible nature - was a key difference as she took control at Flushing Meadows.

Rybakina stayed calm in an opening set where her first serve let her down and, despite her biggest weapon not firing on all cylinders, was able to execute a devastating returning game which left Sabalenka frustrated.

Sabalenka's groundstrokes improved as Rybakina's level dropped slightly in a tighter second set, taking her third opportunity to force a decider when she swarmed over Rybakina's second serve in the 12th game.

But the loose shots from Sabalenka reappeared in the third set - as did the negativity.

Rybakina's deep returning pinned Sabalenka to the baseline as she broke for a 2-1 lead, which allowed the incoming world number one to grow in stature.

There was a sign of nerves when Rybakina produced a double fault on her first championship point, but she reset admirably to hammer down an ace and underline her status as the best player in the world.

From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed

Listen to All About US Open: Rybakina crowned champion as Sabalenka melts down

Rybakina rarely shows emotion on the court but there was a brief flash of a smile as she clinched her second major victory of an outstanding 2026 season.

That illustrated the sense of satisfaction she felt after winning a title few had predicted - not only because she had never previously gone beyond the last 16 in New York but the circumstances coming into the final major of the season.

With her penetrating serve and thunderous groundstrokes, Rybakina has a brand of first-strike tennis that can take the racquet out of anyone's hands.

Therefore it has been a surprise she has not enjoyed greater success on the Flushing Meadows hard courts, perhaps a result of her personality not being particularly suited to the brash nature of New York.

"I was coming here for the last 10 years and it was never successful. I'm falling in love with New York more and more," Rybakina, 27, said.

What makes the second seed's victory even more remarkable is that she was unsure if she would be fit enough to even play.

Rybakina was unable to walk for several days after injuring her ankle in the Cincinnati Open quarter-finals, putting her chances of competing here in serious jeopardy.

Not only was Rybakina able to play, but she cruised through her opening four matches thanks to a huge service game that rarely allowed opponents to get into points.

Rybakina's next two wins over China's Zheng Qinwen and home favourite Coco Gauff required more work after losing the first sets, proving she had the durability to come through tough battles.

Against Sabalenka, she showed both facets of her game, bullying her from the baseline and digging in when necessary to leave her only a French Open title away from the career Grand Slam.

"Some magic is happening. I was unlucky with injury and just going day by day," Rybakina told Sky Sports.

"We didn't know how it was going to be so I'm super happy and still can't believe it."

The chance to beat the woman who had taken her number one ranking was extra motivation for Sabalenka.

However, it was evident from the early stages that the stress of the situation was still troubling the four-time major singles champion - and Rybakina's superb return of serve in the early exchanges only exacerbated it.

The pressure Sabalenka was feeling manifested in some aggressive second serves, and it was unsurprising to see one go long for a double fault on the decisive break point in the opening set.

While Sabalenka showed the resilience which she has demonstrated in her ascent to the top of the sport, she never looked completely at ease.

Dramatic displays of emotion designed to let off steam - yelling, flinging her arms in the air, bouncing her racquet off the court and hiding underneath her towel - were not enough to help produce a gutsy victory which would have ranked among her best.

Instead she will have to come to terms with another near miss at a Grand Slam.

It was Sabalenka's fifth defeat from nine majors final and provides further weight to the argument that she has underachieved at the biggest tournaments given her dominance on the WTA Tour.

"The last thing I want to do right now is give a speech but I will try my best," an emotional Sabalenka told the 24,000 crowd on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I wish I could have performed a little bit better, but I guess next year."

title: Scientists Create a New Form of Ice at More Than 2000°C
description: Water is one of the most commonplace, essential substances in the human world.
fullText:
Water is one of the most commonplace, essential substances in the human world.

We literally can't function without its properties as a near-universal solvent. It falls from the sky. We bathe in it, drink it, and immerse ourselves in it for fun.

But if just considered as a liquid, water is extremely weird, behaving in ways completely at odds with other liquids. It becomes less dense when it freezes. Its surface tension is bizarrely high. So is its boiling point. And, based on its molecular weight, it should be a gas at room temperature.

And that's all at normal, ambient Earth conditions.

Tweak the pressure and the temperature a few notches, and water's outlandish behavior gets even more out of hand.

Scientists have now demonstrated one of the weirdest forms of ice yet – under preposterous pressures up to 2.3 million atmospheres, and tremendous temperatures up to 2,630 kelvins (2,357 degrees Celsius, or 4,274 degrees Fahrenheit).

At those temperatures, you'd normally expect water to emphatically be a gas – even partially sundered into its constituent oxygen and hydrogen atoms. But something interesting happens at the astronomical pressures found deep inside planets.

When water transitions from a liquid to a gas, or vapor, it expands. Under crushing pressures of millions of atmospheres, this expansion is stymied. Instead, water can remain extraordinarily dense, taking on exotic forms unlike any ice we encounter at Earth's surface.

One of these is superionic ice – a deeply odd state of matter that's neither entirely solid nor entirely liquid. Its oxygen atoms remain fixed in a rigid crystal lattice, as they would in a solid. But the hydrogen nuclei are mobile, diffusing through that lattice more like particles in a liquid.

At slightly different sets of conditions, the arrangement of the oxygen atoms shifts into different configurations known as phases. There are some twenty-something known phases of water ice, a few of which become superionic under extreme conditions. Scientists are always looking for more.

And it's not just weirdness for weirdness's sake. Superionic ice is thought to exist deep inside Uranus and Neptune, where its unusual properties may play a role in generating the planets' equally unusual magnetic fields.

In their new experiments, a team led by physicist Alexis Forestier of the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission subjected tiny samples of water to the sorts of extreme conditions expected in the interiors of ice giant planets.

They squeezed the samples between the tips of diamonds to pressures as high as 230 gigapascals, while using lasers to heat them to thousands of degrees. That's 2.3 million times Earth's atmospheric pressure at sea level – the pressure at the center of Earth, for context, is around 360 gigapascals.

Then, using an extremely narrow beam of synchrotron X-rays, they probed for changes in the crystal structure of the ice.

What emerged was a configuration predicted theoretically but never unambiguously observed in experiments: hexagonal close-packed, or hcp, ice. As the hcp crystal was heated, its expansion also showed a signature of superionic behavior, suggesting it entered the superionic state at around 1,700 kelvins.

The name refers to the arrangement of the oxygen atoms. Imagine you're packing identical balls in layers; there are a number of different ways those layers can be stacked while packing the balls as tightly as possible.

One previously identified form of superionic ice has a face-centered cubic, or fcc, structure.

In the newly identified hcp ice, the layers are stacked in a different sequence. The researchers found evidence that one can transform into the other as the layers shift position.

This transformation seems to occur as conditions grow more extreme.

At 155 gigapascals and 2,000 kelvins, the signal observed from the X-ray probe was a mix of fcc and hcp.

Dialing up to 197 gigapascals and 2,250 kelvins, the hcp signature became stronger relative to fcc.

Intriguingly, this may not have been the first time the researchers had produced hcp ice.

Looking back at data from an earlier experiment, they realized that a previously unidentified X-ray diffraction peak observed above 130 gigapascals was likely the signature of hcp ice – they just hadn't recognized it at the time.

Their results suggest that, at pressures above around 200 gigapascals, hcp may become the more stable arrangement of superionic ice.

It seems like a relatively small change – literally on the atomic scale – but the difference could mean big things for the Solar System.

If hcp ice conducts electricity differently from fcc ice, its presence deep inside Uranus and Neptune could change models of how material and electrical charge move through their interiors – processes thought to be involved in generating the planets' strange, messy, lopsided magnetic fields.

We don't actually know about the properties of hcp ice yet, though. The stuff has only just been discovered.

The researchers invite further theoretical work to tease apart those properties – especially its mechanical plasticity and electrical conductivity.

Further experiments will also be needed to pin down exactly where, across the extremes of pressure and temperature, hcp ice is stable relative to its fcc counterpart.

Water is really weird, and superionic ice is even weirder.

Scientists have only just scratched the surface of what this strange molecule can do; in a way, it feels fitting that we need to rely on it to stay alive.

Stay frosty, water. Or hot. You do you.

The findings have been published in Physical Review Letters.

title: South Africa cap series victory over New Zealand with win in Baltimore
description: South Africa complete a 3-1 series win over New Zealand as the world champions' consistency, power and cohesion proves too much in the fourth Test in Baltimore.
fullText:
Rugby's Greatest Rivalry - Fourth Test

Tries: de Allende (2), van den Berg, PS du Toit, Arendse, Hanekom Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu (2), van den Berg, Libbok (2) Pens: Feinberg-Mngomezulu

Tries: Taylor, Jordan, Blackadder, B Barrett Cons: McKenzie (4)

South Africa completed a 3-1 series win over New Zealand as the world champions' consistency, power and cohesion once again proved too much in the fourth Test in Baltimore.

After victory in the series opener in Johannesburg last month, the All Blacks jumped to the top of the world rankings and threatened to shake up rugby's world order.

However, South Africa clawed their way back to triumph - just as their director of rugby Rassie Erasmus had predicted.

While New Zealand were spirited and skilful in pursuit of a win to square the series, the Springboks' go-forward up front and the depth of their bench kept the All Blacks at bay.

The match played out in front of a near-capacity crowd of 68,173 at the M&T Bank Stadium, the largest-ever crowd to watch a rugby match in the USA.

A successful stateside excursion completes a series that has been compelling viewing and stress-tested both sides' aspirations of lifting the Rugby World Cup next year - the two nations have won the past five editions of the tournament.

It was New Zealand who started fastest in Maryland on Saturday.

Eight minutes in, their breathtakingly quick tiki-taka catch-pass, with the backline holding their depth, outflanked South Africa's blitz defence to set up the first try of the match for hooker Codie Taylor.

However, the Springboks' brute strength in the close quarters meant they could collect points without needing to resort to such high-risk passages of play.

With their forward pack on top in the scrum and winning collisions, Damian de Allende burrowed over from short range, before scrum-half Morne van den Berg flashed a dummy and darted past Sam Darry for a similar score.

Those tries opened up a 17-7 lead for the Springboks. With Eben Etzebeth crunching returning New Zealand fly-half Richie Mo'unga in the tackle and Jasper Wiese stampeding around in the loose, the Boks seemed poised to stretch away and out of sight.

Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who had pushed a long-range penalty to the right of the uprights early on, missed a drop-goal shot. An overcooked attempt to find the corner also cost his team.

New Zealand's combination of hard toil and sparkling hands then bought them a way back into the game just before half-time.

Will Jordan, his nation's all-time leading try-scorer, streaked off his wing on a superb line to dunk down over the line at the end of 32 draining phases.

Four points down at the break, Dave Rennie's side had hopes of taking home half of a specially-designed series trophy, which, held together by magnets, can be shared between the two sides.

But South Africa ensured that innovation went unused.

Malcolm Marx trundled over at the back of a rolling maul after the interval and, three minutes later, Pieter-Steph du Toit barged over after a sharp blindside break by the impressive Van den Berg.

Ethan Blackadder's score in the final quarter cut the Boks' lead to eight points, but South Africa hit the accelerator once again as the toll taken by a high-paced match and a long tour caught up on both teams and space opened up.

Kurt-Lee Arendse sliced through open field after Damian McKenzie had broken through in the opposite direction, but Josh Moorby failed to gather his pass.

Four minutes later, Cameron Hanekom scooped up scrappy ball to put the result beyond doubt and render replacement Beauden Barrett's late try only a footnote.

title: Hodgkinson second to Werro after hamstring tear
description: Keely Hodgkinson is again denied a major prize by rival Audrey Werro - but reveals she had to overcome a torn hamstring to make the start line at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship.
fullText:
Keely Hodgkinson was again denied a major prize by rival Audrey Werro - but revealed she had overcome a torn hamstring to make the start line at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

Britain's Olympic 800m champion sustained the injury while competing in the European Championship final less than a month ago, when she was dethroned by 22-year-old Swiss sensation Werro.

Hodgkinson was forced to miss Diamond League races in Zurich and Brussels, and said following her second-place finish in Budapest that it was "touch and go" whether she would be fit to compete at the sport's new global event.

Werro controlled Saturday's 800m race from start to finish, winning in one minute 55.88 seconds to underline her position as the event's current leading athlete.

Despite her injury setback, Hodgkinson overtook Femke Broeders-Bol on the home straight for second in 1:56.26.

"On the outside, people might think I'm disappointed - but I'm actually quite proud of how I approached that," Hodgkinson told BBC Sport.

"When was Europeans? Four weeks ago. I unfortunately tore my hamstring during that race, so I didn't know if I was going to be here.

"It's been a bit of a frustrating season but, I think overall, I'm finishing second in the world and I can't really be too hard on myself for that."

Recap Ultimate Championship day two: Second-place finishes for Hodgkinson and Hunter Bell

Ultimate Championship - full results

Each time the leading women's 800m trio have met this season, it has been billed as one of the races of the year. Each time, it has delivered enthralling action.

Since beginning 2026 with a dominant indoor season in which she won world indoor gold and broke the indoor 800m world record, Hodgkinson has been second-best in meetings with Werro.

Making remarkable progress in her first season as a full-time athlete, Werro continues to uncover what, increasingly, appears to be potential of history-making proportions since completing her university studies.

Forty-three years had passed since a woman had run a sub-1:54 800m before this season. Werro achieved that three times this summer to close in on Jarmila Kratochvilova's 1983 record of 1:53.28.

Although not required to go as fast on this occasion, she showed her maturity by controlling the final before surging to victory.

Hodgkinson will be pleased to have still had enough to overhaul two-time world 400m hurdles champion Broeders-Bol, who has made rapid progress in her first season since switching events.

On her burgeoning rivalry with Werro and Broeders-Bol, Hodgkinson said: "I honestly love it. I think it's really great for our sport and for women's sport to have so many amazing women pushing each other.

"I'm happy to be part of it. Hopefully, next time, I'll come out on top.

"I'm always there fighting. That's something to be proud of and take into the future. I'm only 24 and hopefully I'll be around for a lot longer."

Although she missed out on the title, Hodgkinson, who will end her season at Athlos next weekend, pocketed $75,000 (£55,000) for her efforts.

Athletes are competing for the biggest prize pot in the sport's history at the Ultimat Championship, with a total of $10m (£7.4m) on offer across three days of action.

It is hoped that the condensed, innovative format, introduced to bring together the world's best athletes at the end of a season which otherwise would have lacked a global championship, can help shape the sport's future.

Vivaldi, Reiki and sauna sessions with training partner Hodgkinson.

That is how Georgia Hunter Bell reset to go agonisingly close to her fourth major title of a sensational season.

The 32-year-old's remarkable return to the sport she had given up until late 2022 continued with European, Commonwealth and world indoor gold medals this year.

But a busy season for Hunter Bell - this was the Olympic bronze medallist's 20th race - appeared to catch up with her at last week's Diamond League final, where she faded to fourth.

After finishing runner-up to Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska by 0.17 seconds in a brilliant head-to-head down the home straight in Hungary, Hunter Bell - who clocked 3:57.72 - told BBC Sport: "I'm so proud of myself. I've done absolutely everything I could this year.

"I had to get myself into a stronger place mentally after last week. I didn't have the buzz that I usually do walking out.

"I listened to a lot of Vivaldi's Spring, a very hopeful song. I did Reiki to try and get rid of any bad energy.

"I went to the spa with Keely - she made me sit in the sauna for like 20 minutes and sweat out all the bad energy. And I worked with my coaches to get my belief and hunger back. It was definitely there today on the home straight."

In Saturday's penultimate race, Amy Hunt was disappointed by her eighth-place finish in a stacked women's 100m final, won by American world champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden ahead of Olympic gold medallist Julien Alfred.

After winning her first individual global medal with 200m silver last year, the 24-year-old achieved a historic four gold medals at last month's Europeans.

The next challenge, and ultimately Hunt's ambition, is to replicate that on the global stage - but she was unable to get close to Jefferson-Wooden, who triumphed in a world-leading 10.62 seconds, the joint-seventh fastest time in history.

Hunt, who will return for the 200m on Sunday, told BBC Sport: "I feel a bit disassociated right now. That's the first time dealing with having a 100m semi, then having to regroup and go back out [for the final].

"I don't think that I did myself very proud in that race but I'm lucky to be able to go to sleep tonight and come back out tomorrow in my more favourite event and see what happens."

European champion Matthew Hudson-Smith faded to fifth in 44.28 seconds in the men's 400m final, as Botswana's Collen Kebinatshipi's ran the joint-fifth fastest time in history in 43.39.

title: Ingebrigtsen withdraws from 1500m showdown with Kerr
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen will not contest the men's 1500m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, putting his reunion with rival Josh Kerr on hold.
fullText:
Jakob Ingebrigtsen has withdrawn from the 1500m at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, putting his reunion with rival Josh Kerr on hold.

Two-time Olympic gold medallist Ingebrigtsen took an impressive victory in the men's 5,000m final at the inaugural edition of the sport's new global event on Friday night.

But, having only returned to action last month following an 11-month injury lay-off that included Achilles surgery, the 25-year-old Norwegian has announced he does not want to risk competing again in Sunday's 1500m final.

In a video posted on Instagram, Ingebrigtsen said: "Unfortunately I'm not in a position to go in back-to-back races.

"I would love for it to be different, and to be sharper in terms of recovery, but coming from a very difficult last two years with injury problems and Achilles surgery I am forced to be more sensible than I would like to be.

"Ultimately, it is about getting back into racing, getting back to 100% fitness, and thinking about 2027.

"Just looking back a short time ago, it is unbelievable that we have been able to get this far in 2026 and be able to be here."

It did not take long for Ingebrigtsen to make a statement following his return - both on and off the track.

After winning European 5,000m gold in his first race since the World Championships in September 2025, Ingebrigtsen reignited his war of words with Kerr.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Ingebrigtsen criticised Kerr's decision to miss the Europeans, claiming athletes who choose to miss major competitions are "ruining" the sport.

In Budapest on Sunday, he was set for an eagerly anticipated first head-to-head against 2023 world champion Kerr in two years.

Kerr has since responded to those comments, saying Ingebrigtsen's return was "great" for the event - but added that he could "foresee some struggling" for his rival as he continues to rebuild his fitness.

Sunday's men's 1500m final will still pit Kerr against a world-class line-up including Olympic champion Cole Hocker and bronze medallist Yared Nuguse, reigning world champion Isaac Nader, and 2022 world champion Jake Wightman.

Earlier, Ingebrigtsen said he believes he has been "misunderstood" after being criticised for his recent comments, which also included branding his rivals "losers" and "a bunch of cowards".

Those comments came after he attempted to front-run the Diamond League Final but faded to fourth, with the Norwegian angry at his rivals - particularly Hocker - for their reluctance to push the pace.

Speaking after winning the 5,000m title on Friday, Ingebrigtsen said: "I think it's misunderstood just because you ask a question and because you are critical to someone's [actions].

"I think it's what we have to do. We have to have an open dialogue and communication on things that we feel are right or wrong.

"If opening your mouth is creating a war or a fight, then that's not my problem."

title: USS Cole commander recalls chilling 9/11 warning at CIA just 20 minutes before first plane hit
description: Kirk Lippold warned CIA officials that a catastrophic attack was coming just 20 minutes before the first plane struck the World Trade Center.
fullText:
Just 20 minutes before the first hijacked plane struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, the USS Cole's former commander made a chilling prediction inside CIA headquarters.

Speaking on the "Fox News Rundown" podcast commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11, retired Navy Commander Kirk Lippold said the moment at Langley underscores a lesson he believes the nation cannot afford to forget.

Lippold said he had just finished a briefing with a senior CIA official about intelligence related to the USS Cole attack. When asked for his assessment, Lippold warned that it would likely take a catastrophic event on U.S. soil for the American people to recognize the threat.

For 'Horrible Moment,' Bush White House Thought Us Military Shot Down Flight 93

"I said, 'I'm [going to] be honest with you, sir. America doesn't understand. I believe it is going to take a seminal event probably in this country where hundreds, if not thousands, died before Americans realized that we are at war with this guy,' meaning [Osama] bin Laden," Lippold told Fox News' Lucas Tomlinson.

"Twenty minutes after I said that, the first plane hit the North Tower, and I was literally leaving the headquarters when the plane hit the South Tower."

25 Years Later, 9/11 Memories Endure As Nation Gathers To Honor Nearly 3,000 Lives Lost

The 9/11 terror attacks killed nearly 3,000 people, and thousands more have died from related illnesses. Less than a year before that day, Lippold was the commanding officer of the USS Cole when al Qaeda terrorists attacked the guided-missile destroyer.

On Oct. 12, 2000, two suicide bombers in a small boat pulled alongside the ship in Aden, Yemen, offering friendly gestures before detonating explosives in their boat alongside the Cole. Seventeen U.S. sailors were killed, and 37 others were injured in the blast, which ripped a hole near the ship's waterline.

America Built A Fortress After 9/11; Then The Threat Started Hiding In Plain Sight

That incident was one of several al Qaeda attacks in the years leading up to 9/11, including the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings in East Africa, when Lippold argues went largely unanswered by U.S. leadership. For Lippold, watching the Pentagon burn on 9/11 reinforced his belief that the United States must aggressively confront terrorist groups around the globe.

"It really solidified to me the costs that if the United States does not react to the threat of terrorism and countries who support it, we will continue to pay a price in the future," Lippold said.

9/11 Widow Terry Strada Accuses Us Of Protecting Saudi Arabia 25 Years After Terror Attacks, Addresses Vance

"And it really doesn't matter whether it is through the drugs, whether it's through actually [an] attack, through waterborne or vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices, terrorism has to be ruthlessly stopped anywhere around the world," he added.

title: 'Absolute joke' to be worried - Mitchell on England's response
description: England produce dominant second-half performance to comfortably defeat Australia at CorpAcq Stadium in the opening game of the new WXV Global Series.
fullText:
