England produced a dominant second-half performance to defeat Australia at CorpAcq Stadium in the opening game of the new WXV Global Series.

The world champions, playing their first game since winning a record eighth successive Women's Six Nations title in May, were made to work for victory in Salford after trailing at half-time for the first time since 2020.

The Wallaroos led 10-5 at the break, with player of the match Abi Burton scoring England's only try in an error-strewn first half.

John Mitchell's side responded emphatically after the interval, scoring seven tries to quickly put any prospect of a shock defeat to bed and extend their record winning run to 39 matches in front of a crowd of 9,251.

The England head coach described the fixture as "a good pre-season game" after it kicked off the 2026-27 campaign for his players.

"It was the first pre-season game of the year where we had the reality of playing rugby and had to solve [problems], which is good for us," Mitchell told BBC Sport.

"It is an absolute joke if you are worried about being down 10-5. More important is how we worked our way back into it.

"We got 23 players with rugby [into them], and it was a 43-point second half."

During a dominant 20-minute spell, May Campbell, captain Meg Jones, Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya all crossed for tries.

Lucy Packer and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald also then scored, with Australia's Asoiva Karpani adding to Faliki Pohiva's first-half try.

The WXV Global Series has replaced the WXV competition, with England having won both editions of the premier section, WXV1, in 2023 and 2024.

Running from 2026 to 2028, the series features the world's top 12 teams and is designed to provide more competitive matches before the 2029 World Cup in Australia.

The Red Roses face Canada at Exeter's Sandy Park next weekend, the teams' first meeting since England won last year's Rugby World Cup final, before facing New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on 26 September.

"They're great rivals [Canada], a fantastic rugby team, well-coached, a different team to Australia," Mitchell added.

"We only have a very short turnaround. With this being our first pre-season game, lots of players got rugby, so we'll be in a great place."

England blitz Australia in second half to maintain winning run - reaction & try clips

This was the first game with the new women's size 4.5 ball, which is 3% smaller than the standard size five.

In May, England fly-half Zoe Harrison, arguably the best goal-kicker in the women's game, said introducing the ball was "the worst decision someone has ever made".

Scrum-half Samantha Wood confidently drilled over an early penalty as Australia, like they did against England in Brighton in last year's World Cup, started quicker.

Sloppy handling and inaccuracy in the Wallaroos' 22 held back Mitchell's side in the first half.

Burton's try came from slick handling and interplay, indicating what new attack coach Emily Scarratt is trying to implement, even if England were not at their brightest early on.

"The message at half-time was we know that we weren't at our best, so we knew we needed to come out and rip back into them and give it to them physically because they came out absolutely gunning," Burton told BBC Sport.

"At the end that cohesiveness started to kick in.

"There's so much more to come from this team, just a few teething issues we needed to sort out."

Both sides had tries disallowed in the first half, but Australia scrambled brilliantly in defence to take a deserved lead into the break.

The Red Roses have often started slowly under Mitchell before clicking into gear, with the power of their bench a level above the rest.

However, England had not trailed at half-time since a match against France in November 2020.

Mitchell said that, without a "tournament to win", his side have to be "very patient" in how they approach these Test matches.

With a shock defeat potentially looming, his side turned to their destructive maul to power over the line before a scrum penalty gave them valuable field position.

A clever grubber kick from Sale Sharks' Holly Aitchison, on her 50th cap, then found Jones as the combination of power and backline skill finally came together.

When in need of a try, the Red Roses maul tends to deliver more often than not.

It was England's pack that dominated Canada to win the World Cup, and it delivered again through Field to give them some breathing room.

England, with the likes of Hannah Botterman and Marlie Packer coming off the bench, continued to grow into the game as their accuracy improved while Australia tired.

Both wingers crossed to underline the balance in play that has made Mitchell's side so difficult to beat.

Harrison also nailed three conversions, underlining a successful adjustment to the new ball.

Both Canada and New Zealand will pose more of a threat in attack and will take note of how Australia made life difficult for the Red Roses in the first half.

But it is yet another win for a side who, simply put, seem to know little else.

title: How can India qualify for the WTC final 2027? Qualification scenario, points and wins required to reach World Test Championship final
description: The Sporting News takes a look at the WTC 2027 Final qualification scenario for India.
fullText:
India's road to the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) Final 2027 has become much clearer following the recent Tests that were played.

As every match affects the percentage points table (PCT), India still finds themselves in the race, but with very little to spare as they move forward towards the end of the cycle.

In the first of the two Tests that India played against Sri Lanka, the visitors registered a massive 165-run victory in Galle and then aimed to complete a whitewash. However, a valiant performance from Sri Lanka in the final day of the 2nd Test in Colombo helped them to hold the visitors to a draw in the final match of the series.

After a surprise win over Australia in the first Test, Bangladesh succumbed to an embarrassing loss in the second and final match of the series in Mackay. Till date, Bangladesh hold on to the fourth position but India can overtake them if they win the second match.

England moved to the sixth position, replacing Sri Lanka after their 3-0 whitewash win over Pakistan on September 12.

In this article, The Sporting News takes an in-depth look at India's WTC 2027 Final Qualification scenario.

India failed to capitalise on the away tour of Sri Lanka. While they won the series, they failed to complete a whitewash and remained fifth on the points table.

However, their prospects of securing themselves among the top two will also be contingent on the performance of the other teams.

fullText:
CBF mourns the passing of Paulo Angioni, Fluminense football director and Brazil National Team supervisor at the 1990 World Cup Credits: CBF

The Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF) deeply mourns the passing this Saturday (12) of Paulo Angioni, Fluminense's executive football director and supervisor of the Brazilian National Team at the 1990 World Cup, and extends its condolences to the executive's family, friends, and fans. He was 80 years old and had been battling pancreatic cancer.

"Today we lost a pioneer, an executive who worked tirelessly for the professionalization and modernization of Brazilian football, always with great ethics and respect. Paulo Angioni leaves behind a legacy of dedication to football and appreciation for the human side of athletes, coaching staff, and club employees. In tribute to his victorious history, CBF will observe a minute of silence in all stadiums across Brazil this weekend," said CBF president Samir Xaud.

A native of Rio de Janeiro, born on June 5, 1946, the Rio-born executive had been active in football for four decades. He worked at several clubs in the country, including Palmeiras, Flamengo, Vasco, Bahia, Corinthians, and Olaria. At the time, he already served as football director, a position that would gain relevance and prominence over the years.

At Fluminense, the club he supported, he had four spells, the last beginning in 2018. During that period, he helped the club win a series of titles, including the 2022 and 2023 Rio de Janeiro State Championships, the 2023 CONMEBOL Libertadores, and the 2024 CONMEBOL Recopa.

In his role, Angioni was known and valued for building relationships of respect and care with the employees and athletes of the clubs he worked for. In its official statement, Fluminense highlighted this human side of the executive.

"His contribution to the development of young players will be remembered by many, and his lessons will remain with us as an example of life, compassion, and solidarity," the club wrote in its statement.

title: 'Red rag to a bull' - Sabalenka's extra motivation to win US Open
description: Aryna Sabalenka has lost the world number one ranking to Elena Rybakina - but has the chance to take revenge in the US Open final.
fullText:
Aryna Sabalenka was fully aware she would have to win the US Open to stand any chance of stopping Elena Rybakina overtaking her as world number one.

Even that would not necessarily be enough. And as the pair prepare to meet in Saturday's final, Sabalenka knows her 99-week stay at the top of the world rankings is at an end.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina is assured of replacing Sabalenka at the top of the rankings, guaranteeing that by reaching the semi-finals.

Having also beaten the Belarusian to win this year's Australian Open title, Rybakina now has the opportunity to inflict further damage.

But that provides extra motivation for Sabalenka before their fourth meeting of the year.

"It is going to be red rag to a bull for her - she is not going to be happy," said former British number one Annabel Croft on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Now she has the opportunity to end this year on a high."

Sabalenka, who has beaten Rybakina in Indian Wells and Miami since the Melbourne final, still has history in her sights as she bids to become only the third woman in the Open era to win the New York singles title three years in a row.

The four-time Grand Slam champion's victory over American third seed Jessica Pegula in the semi-finals was her finest display in months, playing with a fire and freedom that had been missing previously.

Afterwards, Sabalenka played down the significance of losing her ranking, joking she did not care about it.

But she clearly does. Sabalenka's coach Anton Dubrov said as much when he spoke about how the issue has been hanging over her.

"I actually like this [losing the ranking] happened. It's ended and it's extra fuel," Dubrov said.

"There is no more extra draining [of mental energy] or thinking about it.

"There's a next chapter right now. You have to chase again. It's extra motivation for you. Just go and get it."

Sabalenka might have arrived in New York as the two-time defending champion, but there were concerns about her game and mindset.

Over the past five months, the 28-year-old had lost a series of matches from strong positions against opponents she was expected to beat.

The most notable was in the French Open quarter-finals. Sabalenka held a commanding set and a double break lead against 25th seed Diana Shnaider before capitulating to a 3-6 7-5 6-0 defeat.

Earlier in the clay-court season, Sabalenka blew six match points against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid and let slip a first-set lead over Sorana Cirstea in Rome, demonstrating a lack of mental focus that she had not shown on the WTA Tour for a long time.

A chink of vulnerability was still apparent during this North American hard-court swing, when she held clear advantages against 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek at the Cincinnati Open before losing in straight sets.

But there was no panic for Sabalenka or her team, says her high performance coach Jason Stacy.

"We all understand that this is just part of the thing," Stacy said.

"We just give her space to be herself, help her figure out what might work for her right now.

"Giving her that freedom, but also knowing that she has the guidance of all of us, I think that just gives her a power that few are lucky enough to have."

For different reasons, two-time major champion Rybakina also came into the US Open with serious doubts about her chances.

Turning her ankle during the Cincinnati quarter-finals left the 27-year-old unable to walk for several days afterwards and put her chances of even competing at Flushing Meadows in jeopardy.

However, not only was the 2022 Wimbledon champion able to play, but she cruised through her opening four matches thanks to a huge service game which rarely allowed opponents to get into points.

Rybakina's past two wins against China's Zheng Qinwen and home favourite Coco Gauff proved she has the durability - in baseline exchanges and physical scraps - to withstand pressure.

"She wasn't even hitting balls three weeks ago," Croft said.

"What was interesting is that she said she worked on other things with her team and talked a lot and did a lot of work without hitting tennis balls.

"I presume she meant mental preparation and she has brought the freshness into this tournament."

The pair contesting the US Open final means they will close the Grand Slam season as they began it in the Australian Open's showpiece match.

"Talking about Grand Slams, it feels like a last push of the season," Sabalenka, who is aiming for her first major title of 2026, added.

"The mentality is just 'I'm ready'. I'm ready for whatever it's going to take to get the win."

title: Naomi Klein: ‘Extreme wealth has a deranging effect. It turns you into a supremacist’
description:

fullText:
She’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explains how the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of power

Naomi Klein’s new book starts on a mountaintop with two “faithful men gathering an audience to share their vision”. It’s a vision of a paradise city, gated at every entrance, no need for weapons there, everyone in it rich. One of the men has tears in his eyes as he describes its beauty. The opening scene of End Times Fascism, co-written with Astra Taylor, is not a metaphor, however. The men are Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The year is 2026, the mountain is Davos. The paradise city will be called New Gaza.

The World Economic Forum get-together in Davos, Switzerland, has always had a twin purpose – to provide a platform for the super-rich to describe all the good they are doing on poverty and climate, and to give us a glimpse into their enviable lives. This year what we witnessed was, quite brazenly, the world’s richest men gathering to discuss the real estate possibilities of a mass grave.

At that same Davos, Donald Trump announced his Board of Peace for the reconstruction of Gaza – it has delivered nothing substantial in the seven months since, but more significantly, Klein says, “we’re being hit with so many extraordinary events that it’s hard to hold on to what a big deal it is: they have announced a privatised United Nations”.

“I think we understand that wealth compounds, right? Certainly rich people understand that wealth compounds,” Klein continues, speaking to me from her peaceful, roomy study in British Columbia. “But I don’t feel like we spend a lot of time really thinking about the implications of what it means for that much wealth to be compounded, and what that does psychologically. Part of the new shamelessness we’re seeing is just what happens when this amount of financial, mediagenic, technological and military weaponry is concentrated in the hands of this very small, unaccountable group of people. They stop trying to seduce us in any way.”

Klein looks calm and curious as she delivers this message. She has a ready laugh. But then, she had the same unruffled, buoyant delivery when I interviewed her on stage in Manchester for Doppelgänger, her 2023 book in which she described how the digital world is destroying our connection to reality, and one another. In 1999, when her breakthrough work No Logo was published, she seemed exhilaratingly certain, at 29, that neoliberalism was bringing harm that we couldn’t yet even see the extent of, and nonetheless appeared centred and happy in the world. Somehow she manages to maintain this attitude, even though the news she delivers is always so convincingly, unbelievably bad.

End Times Fascism describes the world we’re in, where the components of authoritarianism are modelled everywhere you look: anarcho-libertarian economics in Argentina, the destruction of a free press in Russia, the erosion of democratic institutions in Hungary (until Viktor Orbán was deposed), “anti-immigrant neofascism” in Italy, the weaponisation of trans identity by Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Islamophobia in Modi’s India. But this is fascism with a difference. Its proponents are actively willing an apocalypse, or a wave of interconnected apocalypses brought forth by climate change and financial chaos, to hasten us towards a post-democratic world in which only a rich few survive to prosper.

This book started as an article in the Guardian, “which went totally viral,” Klein says. “Astra and I knew there was a lot more reporting to do, but on a personal level, did we want to spend the next year in the minds of these people, in these cultures? Then Astra said, ‘I’m down the rabbit hole, I’m gonna be listening to these guys anyway. So I may as well feel like I’m doing something about it.’ This is the reason it’s the first book I’ve co-written. When you go to dark, scary places, it’s nice to bring a friend.” Astra Taylor is also a writer, activist and documentary maker, and founded the Debt Collective, a fascinating experiment in building structured, quasi-unionised solidarity around personal debt, with the long term goals of abolishing student tuition fees, nationalising healthcare and building tenant power.

In the book, Klein and Taylor introduce us to the religious fundamentalists, Christian Zionists and Christian Nationalists in the US, readying themselves for the second coming. Describing a “bunkered state”, the authors connect climate-related disasters, a rabid anti-immigrant standing army in the form of ICE and a politics built on false promises and misinformation to depict a febrile, riven society that doesn’t know what to believe. But the truly terrifying bit is the bridging section, on tech billionaires. The super-rich have apocalypse fantasies of their own, built not on faith or ideology but on a calm and rational evaluation of how best to maintain their position; they would genuinely rather reign in hell than share in heaven. And they have all the money to make sure they get there.

“These are trends I’ve been following for a long time,” Klein says. “The privatised enclave born of shock, of disaster, I saw when I was reporting from Iraq. There’s the image of the Green Zone, this Emerald City run by the US in the middle of Baghdad, built by Halliburton and all of these private contractors, with the power to appoint a viceroy. In the final parts of The Shock Doctrine [2007], I talk about how these contractors migrated [from Iraq] to Hurricane Katrina, and the idea that these climate disasters are their next growth frontier. Reporters started calling New Orleans ‘Baghdad on the Bayou’. The gang’s all here, there’s Halliburton, there’s Bechtel, there’s Blackwater.”

But, and she cannot stress this enough, as useful as it is to know the recent history of these trends, you should not take comfort from the idea that you’ve seen it all before. “I have found the image of a spiral really useful, in terms of how to make sense of the fact that our era is both familiar and different,” Klein says. “The thing about a spiral is that you’re going round, but you’re not going to the same place. If the spiral is pointing down, it’s deeper, it’s tighter, it’s carrying more velocity, it’s carrying more force, it’s carrying more heat, it’s carrying more violence.” The image is at once poetic and extremely sobering. She proffers a brief morale boost, like someone handing you a slice of orange on your way into a war zone. “You can flip a spiral – it goes outwards, it’s the spiral of the universe.”

At the moment we’re in now, when crises and disasters hit so frequently that we’re in a constant state of disorientation and shock, the status quo isn’t static, it’s always getting worse. “There’s this impulse to read history,” Klein says. “We’ve seen it again and again. After 9/11, people were suddenly reading history books about Afghanistan and Iraq, Chomsky, trying to find their bearings. We saw it again during the pandemic, people were reading about the plagues of the past. But there’s a trap in believing that everything has happened before, that there is not a compounding effect of history. After Donald Trump was re-elected, I’ll be honest with you, Shock Doctrine sales went crazy. People were saying, ‘It’s exactly like you said,’ and I was thinking, ‘I don’t think it is’.”

The neoliberal age – for brevity let’s call it the period between the end of the cold war and Covid – was “capitalism lying on the couch in its underwear, going ‘what are you gonna do, leave me?’ In the cold war, a little competition went a long way – after the collapse of the Soviet Union, that competition is lost, capitalism stopped trying.” But there was a vulnerability to being super-rich in those days, because whether you’d come by your wealth through privatisation politics in the US or Europe, or by hastier, more kleptocratic means in ex-communist states, it was plainly public wealth that you’d captured. “So they would stage these seduction rituals, whether it was at Davos or Aspen, or at Ted, or the Clinton Global Initiative. They’d say, ‘We are going to cure the sick, and we are going to fund your schools in this new and exciting way, don’t worry about us. Don’t be afraid of our wealth. This is actually a new way of redistributing for the public good.’”

I distinctly remember that world: huge conferences like the Skoll foundation awards, where journalists would be wined and dined while watching immensely rich people hand out £20,000 prizes to grassroots clean water initiatives in Kenya. To be fair, in the era before and directly after the financial crash, there were plenty of dissenting voices about capitalist benevolence solving intractable problems like inequality. Many people, Klein at their vanguard, pointed out that it smelled like a scam. But while we were having that discussion, the wealth agenda moved on.

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, at the Faena Hotel in Miami, Peter Thiel hosted panel discussions titled “the enemy”, naming sustainable development goals, “precautionary principles” and “social responsibility” as those foes, rounded off with an “apocalypse ball”-themed fancy dress party . Some of the costumes, Klein and Taylor write, were “a doctor of eugenics’’; a “Haitian chef with a bloodied cat toy hanging out of his apron [a reference to the Springfield immigrant pet‑eating hoax, which spread in 2024, repeated by both Trump and JD Vance]; a couple wearing pagers as a ha-ha reference to Israel’s murderous attack in Lebanon.”

Thiel has been explicitly anti-democracy for years, writing in 2009, “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” But other tech billionaires have had a complete volte face. “Jeff Bezos renamed a stadium in Seattle the Climate Pledge Arena, and gave out Earth prizes,” Klein points out. Elon Musk invested in electric cars and once saw himself as a saviour figure. “Any time anyone was in trouble, Musk would rush in to save them, ‘I shall save Puerto Rico’, ‘I shall save the children stuck down the mine’. It’s fun to be a superhero, right? But if you’re going to be a superhero, you should be worshipped. And people stopped worshiping them.” Now, the climate pledges are gone, replaced by a performed nihilism around averting climate crisis, coupled with a determination to build ever more data centres. “We’re not dealing with stupid people who don’t understand climate change,” Klein says. “We’re dealing with people who know very clearly what it means to wire together 35 gas turbines in Memphis.” (It means gargantuan energy and water use, as well as the destruction of air and sound quality in the vicinity, all for Musk to power Grok, his intermittently Nazi large language model.)

The speed with which previously Democrat-leaning billionaires fell in behind Trump in 2024 was jaw-dropping. “I don’t think that Mark Zuckerberg’s phase of seeming to care deeply about democracy and climate change was real,” Klein says. “He reincarnates as whatever is good for his business. Figures like Thiel and Musk, where there is real ideology there, are easier to understand than figures like Bezos and Zuckerberg, where it really does feel like there’s no there there, they’re just uninteresting guys that ended up massively rich.” She’s passingly interested in what combination of events created these men, many of whom were forged in the dotcom boom, when they were worshipped as gods, pictured on the cover of Time magazine in gold thrones. There’s an element of ego rage, that we just aren’t grateful enough. Ultimately, though, “we end the book concluding that wealth has its own deranging effects. It almost inevitably turns you into a supremacist because humans are creatures of story and you need a story to rationalise, why you? Why do you have so much in a time of so much want and need? And the only possible story that’s available is that there’s something about you that justifies it.”

There’s a new goading quality to the talking points of the super-rich – explicit eugenicism and Islamophobia, raw delight in the prospect of AI wiping out our jobs. It almost feels as though they’re daring us to rebel, just so that they can prove that rebellion is fruitless.

On that, though, Klein would disagree. It is not beyond our collective means to build a wealth disarmament movement, or a tech disarmament movement. She points to the Pearson brothers, KeShaun and Justin, fighting Musk’s Colossus 2 data centre in Memphis: “the way they so consciously root their struggle in the history of the civil rights movement, and the environmental justice movement in Memphis, going back to the formerly enslaved people who built Boxtown. This is where MLK was murdered, assassinated after marching with the sanitation workers in Memphis.” KeShaun Pearson leads Memphis Community Against Pollution, which has had major wins against oil pipelines, the industrial release of carcinogenic chemicals, and is now mobilising against data centres. Justin is running for Congress.

In End Times Fascism, Klein and Taylor raise Walter Benjamin’s concept “jetztzeit”, literally “now time”, a moment so pregnant with the spirit, the urgency of revolution that it marshals the energy of all movements that went before it. Again, it’s poetic, but it’s also literal, observable. If we want to oppose this new fascist strain, we really have to get a move on. “I don’t tend to use this language, I try to be measured, but I think I’ve earned the right to escalate,” she says. “The moment we’re in, people are really mad and however mad you are, it’s not enough. Because there is something so profound about no longer believing in the future, about seeing no value in our shared home, in the natural world. They’re traitors to creation.”

Klein doesn’t want for reasons to fight. “I’ve made a choice to live very close to nature in a pretty wild part of British Columbia,” she says. “On a dark night, it’s a blanket of stars. And now we see so many of what I call Elon’s space bugs [Starlink satellites] just crawling through the sky. He wants to increase that a hundredfold. Who said he could? Who gave him that right? That’s a place where I find my anger. I get really angry about the stars. I get really angry about the orcas. I get really angry about Gaza. Other people will find their anger somewhere else. We have to find our places of deepest love and fight like hell.”

title: Learnings from 12,000 Agentic Code Reviews
description: Mature organisations monitor CI/CD efficiency and PR bounce-back rates. In the agentic world, how can you measure the performance and efficiency of your software factory?
fullText:
Gymwasp is a Swamp customer, currently in stealth. I helped them get their software factory up and running: the pipeline that orchestrates code planning through to shipped code, agentically using swamp as the harness. No human is reading any code. They've been generous enough to share the metrics that swamp collected on their factory's performance across 372 issues over the span of 6 months, and those metrics are what this post is built on.

They call their factory The Mandible, which correlates well with the factory we run internally for Swamp itself:

A human is in the loop at Plan and Review, but they're not reading code. They're asserting whether the agents understood the problem correctly and making product calls the agents can't make for themselves.

At Plan and Review, all 7 reviewers run in parallel against either the plan or the written code. Each one is a separate agent process on its own model instance, so none can see what the others found. Each reviewer returns a verdict:

The round's overall verdict is the worst of the seven.

Each reviewer gets a narrow brief and an explicit out-of-lane exclusion list. Without exclusion lists, you get the same finding seven times.

Most teams aren't measuring agentic review at all. The few that do are likely measuring either the time it takes to get a change out, or the magnitude of issues they can get through in a timeframe. Neither are useful when looking at optimising the process.

Here's what was tracked, and what it can tell you. The chart below shows the probability an issue has earned a clean pass (all 7 ✅) by review round N.

The gap between the curves is the whole story. Merge readiness arrives almost immediately. 65% of issues have no failing lane after a single round, and 98.9% by round 4. Since warn does not block merge, nearly all the review volume past round 4 is spent chasing a clean pass on a complex PR that is incredibly unlikely given the non-determinism of LLM-based reviews.

Kaplan-Meier estimator. The two curves use different bars: a strict all-lane pass, versus merely no lane failing.

After round 4, extra rounds introduce as much uncertainty as they're trying to fix. Combined with the 218 fails that appeared in lanes which were previously clean, this is a loop introducing about as much as it removes. Each fix touches adjacent concerns, which triggers findings in lanes that were previously quiet.

Given an issue hasn't passed yet, what's the chance it passes on this round? If extra rounds were helping, this would climb. It does neither: it halves and then plateaus.

The grey bars are issues that shipped with warns. They're exactly why a naive average is wrong. If you only count the ones that clean passed, you'll underestimate cost by nearly half. 29% never reached a clean pass. This is their measure of risk tolerance.

Grey bars are censored observations: issues that stopped at that round without ever scoring a pass. They shipped with warns.

Per-issue review cost didn't scale with volume. The pipeline absorbed a 3x increase without the review loop getting more expensive. That's the whole point of deterministic automation: the pipeline holds the shape even as throughput grows.

Every shipped issue plotted at its merge date against the rounds it took, with the monthly median over the top. Below, issues shipped per week.

1,463 rounds on code, 338 on plans. The agent is far more likely to write the code wrong than write the plan wrong. The plan gate catches architectural mistakes before any code exists.

1,801 adversarial review rounds split between plan review (before code) and code review (after implementation).

i. Anthropic Claude Opus was used throughout, moving from 4.6 to 5 as releases landed during the measurement window.

ii. The power of averages here assumes that with a dataset of 372 issues over 6 months, the "average" PR is representative over time.

iii. Every software factory is tailored to its own organisation and needs. Results and findings will vary based on implementation.

Thanks to the absolute legend James Owens for sharing the data (best man at my wedding too, so top lad).

The data doesn't just tell you whether the process is working now. It tells you when it's drifting.

Pass rate per round stops improving means your reviewers are oscillating, not converging. The fix isn't more rounds. It's changing the briefs. Tighten the exclusion lists. Sharpen the failure vocabulary. Make each lane's definition of fail more concrete so the threshold doesn't wobble between rounds.

One lane dominating the fails means either that lane is genuinely catching more problems (good) or its brief is tuned too aggressively (bad). Test coverage at 19.1% is by design, its brief orders it to fail when an integration test is absent. If your observability lane suddenly starts blocking at 15%, something changed, and it probably isn't the code quality.

Infrastructure flakes eroding trust is the quiet killer. 3.7% of The Mandible's verdicts were lost to agent crashes. 8.1% of rounds had at least one lane unassessed. 111 iterations died before writing a verdict. Go check how many of your test flakes died because of CPU pinning or OOMs in your CI runners. Same concept, different domain. In classic CI, when the flake rate climbs the temptation is to comment the tests out because they're providing no value. Here, if your clean code reviewer is failing frequently, the temptation is to remove it. Same instinct, same mistake. Fix the brief, don't kill the lane.

The "Mergeable" criteria requiring more rounds means your loop is getting worse. Round 4 is the elbow in this data, the point where extra rounds stop buying quality. If next month it's round 6, the briefs have drifted, the exclusion lists are stale, or the codebase has moved enough that the anchors are pointing at the wrong files. Same problem, same fix: instrument, measure, retune.

Perfection is a fallacy. 29% of issues shipped without a clean pass. The pipeline caught the structural problems in the first three rounds, and the warns logged everything else. Chasing 100% on a complex PR given the non-determinism of LLM-based reviews is not a productive use of compute. Ship at merge-ready, batch the follow-ups.

I've written and managed literally thousands of CI/CD pipelines across hundreds of production environments. This is CI/CD optimisation pointed at a new target. The mental model transfers because the shape transfers: a deterministic pipeline with measurable stages, each of which can be instrumented, analysed, and improved.

The old discipline was making builds fast and tests reliable. The new discipline is making review accurate and review loops short. The techniques transfer. The tools MUST be different.

That's the project. Every number in this post came out of swamp's data plane as a byproduct of the work, not as archaeology performed afterwards. Swamp is deterministic automation for AI agents: the scaffolding that controls what each reviewer sees, tracks every verdict, and gives you the data to know whether your loop is converging or just spinning. title: Garcia v Benn - welterweight world title fight predictions
description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's WBC welterweight world title fight between Ryan Garcia and Briton Conor Benn.
fullText:
Conor Benn returns to welterweight for the first time since April 2022 to challenge WBC champion Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas.

The 29-year-old Briton is bidding for the crowning moment of his 10-year professional career at T-Mobile Arena.

Benn has won 25 of his 26 fights as a professional and would emulate his father, Nigel, by claiming a WBC title with another victory.

Garcia, 28, is making the first defence of his belt after beating Mario Barrios by decision in February.

The American has picked up 25 victories in his 28-fight career, earning 20 of those wins by knockout, while losing two, with one no-contest.

Live text commentary will begin on Sunday, 13 September at 03:00 BST on the BBC Sport website and app.

BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for the bout.

Benn makes weight - then puts on 32lbs in 12 hours

"This is a really good fight and it's not as one-sided as everyone thinks. I believe Conor Benn's heart is going to come into question and he's going to have to climb off the floor a couple of times.

title: Trey Wingo, Bob Ley look back on hosting ‘SportsCenter’ on 9/11
description: Friday marked 25 years since the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center, and across the sports world there were solemn remembrances as well as celebrations of the heroes that stepped up that day. Trey Wingo used the day to call up Bob Ley, with whom he hosted the 6 p.m. edition of SportsCenter…
fullText:
Friday marked 25 years since the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center, and across the sports world there were solemn remembrances as well as celebrations of the heroes that stepped up that day.

Trey Wingo used the day to call up Bob Ley, with whom he hosted the 6 p.m. edition of SportsCenter on Tuesday, September 11, 2001, and look back on the surreal, traumatic, and life-changing day, and how they almost didn't go on with the show.

"As I'm driving into work that day I'm like, what am I even going to talk about today? What could remotely matter?" Wingo said. "I remember we got into the offices that day and everyone was sort of just thinking about what could we do, what's available, what's this. I was like, 'Hey maybe we should just turn over all of our resources to ABC News, give them everything.'"

Wingo remembered a meeting with Ley and producer Norby Williamson, where they discussed whether or not the show should air that night.

"I was like, I don't think we should do a show. I think it would be disrespectful. All this stuff. Because I was overwhelmed," Wingo said.

Ley was on the other side of the debate.

"I remember you sat dawn and said 'Look, here's what I think. Obviously this is a really traumatic day and we don't know what's going on, but our job as the show of record' — which is what we thought that the six o'clock SportsCenter was at that time, it was the show of record of what was going on in sports that day — you said, 'We need to chronicle this so people can understand, and have a benchmark to know what happened on that day.'"

Wingo concluded by admitting that Ley, and ultimately SportsCenter, made the right call to go on air.

"In hindsight, I was 100% wrong and you were 100% right."

From there, Ley and Wingo continue to share memories from the day itself and the days that followed, both confronting the strangeness that comes with watching something so visceral slowly become a piece of history.

They also remembered the sports moments that brought the country together in the aftermath of the attacks, namely President Bush's first pitch at Yankee Stadium and Mike Piazza's monster home run for the Mets.

title: Razaullah introduces himself as Pakistan thrive in chaos
description: Cancel the tee time at the Belfry, rearrange the trip to Cadbury World and abort the shopping jolly to the Bullring - Pakistan's debutant Razaullah lights up Edgbaston to send third Test into fourth day.
fullText:
Cancel the tee time at the Belfry, rearrange the trip to Cadbury World and abort the shopping jolly to the Bullring.

The reason? Pakistan's new star Razaullah and 'Razball'.

England's bowlers were thwarted by a Pakistan side who mixed batting belligerence with brilliance and instead of a Saturday off must reconvene at Edgbaston for day four.

The brilliance was provided by Razaullah, who produced a dizzying knock to breathe life into the third Test and lift the spirits of Pakistan supporters everywhere. A new hero, a new hope.

Bazball might be on its way out, but Birmingham might just have witnessed the birth of a new phenomenon during two hours of unbridled chaos where the Test debutant made a stunning 81 off 63 balls coming in at number nine.

A raw 21-year-old with just eight first-class matches to his name, selected more as a tearaway fast bowler reminiscent of Waqar Younis, Razaullah was probably not a name on the radar of England's bowlers when he was called up amid wholesale changes made by Pakistan before the final Test.

After some blistering strokeplay when he took down the home side's attack, they certainly know who he is now.

There were shades of Shahid Afridi or Abdul Razzaq in the flamboyant nature of the way Razaullah flayed England to all parts.

He ended up needing to use three different bats at the crease after breaking two with his explosive hitting.

"It's the first time he's been out there for Pakistan ever, and he absolutely lights up the show. This is the attitude that was needed," said former Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja on BBC Test Match Special.

"Someone with a strong body language and who believes in himself. They'll want him playing all formats because he's a natural in mind, body language and attitude. It was a tremendous fightback."

'Out of control' - Cook questions England tactics

England need 130 after thrilling Razaullah hitting

At times when Razaullah - who has one first-class century - was teeing off, England captain Joe Root wore the expression of a chess player waiting for someone to tell him it was his move.

Root stationed eight fielders on the boundary at one point - but it did not deter Razaullah as he brashly swaggered at the crease with the arrogance of youth.

Razaullah's nine sixes is the joint-most ever in a Test innings in England. The other is Ben Stokes' famous 155 with nine against Australia in the Ashes Test in 2023.

He hit as many sixes as Sir Geoffrey Boycott did in his 108-Test career.

Perhaps being so far behind, and expected to capitulate, liberated Pakistan. There was a freedom to their batting hitherto unseen in this series so far.

Shan Masood played with admirable application with a stoic 95 while captain Babar Azam, a weight lifted off his shoulders, made 76.

Yet it was the swashbuckling Razaullah who really captured the imagination.

"England are going to win this Test match, I'm sure," said former England captain Michael Vaughan.

"But Razaullah has given Pakistan cricket some hope. They've unearthed a gem and he will be a superstar for many years."

Even Razaullah's dismissal was pure theatre lapped up by the crowd. Reprieved lbw to Dan Lawrence he danced down the pitch and was stumped next ball.

The young Pakastani left the field to the warmest ovation.

In another world he might have been playing for Cleethorpes in the Yorkshire Cricket Southern Premier League, having signed for the 2026 season only to be called up to a national training camp in May.

Those with tickets for Saturday must have thought the prospect of seeing any play was remote when Pakistan offered a meek surrender on day one.

Steamrolled for 133 just after lunch in Birmingham on Wednesday they looked rudderless against opponents who were ruthless.

Doubtless many punters will have started to make other plans in the expectation this would all be over swiftly, especially when England racked up 453.

Yet with 129 to defend, Pakistan have an outside chance of what would be the most famous of victories.

It's tempting to look at Pakistan cricket through a certain prism, but when moments like these arrive it's impossible not to. Through the emotional wringer again - despair to hope in the space of three days.

"There wouldn't be any person in the world that would've thought we'd go to day four," added Vaughan.

"That is what Pakistan cricket is. They have had a difficult few weeks. The team has been in turmoil. That is why I love Pakistan cricket.

"England will look back at a lot of the tactics and realise they got it wrong. The short stuff, one over of spin, the second new ball with the spinner.

"That day today will make the England team realise there is a long way to go to be world class."

title: Moroccan official told to stop making 2030 final promise
description: Morocco's prime minister tells the head of the country's football federation to stop making promises about the 2030 World Cup final, while the head of the Spanish federation says the showpiece should be played in Spain.
fullText:
Morocco's prime minister has told the head of the country's football federation to stop making promises about the 2030 World Cup final as Spain says they should stage it.

The next men's World Cup will be co-hosted by Morocco, Spain and Portugal, although the opening three matches will be played in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay to mark the competition's 100th anniversary.

While a list of host stadiums has been proposed, the line-up has yet to be finalised, as well as where the showpiece will take place.

Fouzi Lekjaa, president of the Moroccan football federation (RMFF), declared at a political party event Casablanca would have the 'honour' of hosting the game.

Fifa, world football's governing body and organisers of the World Cup, said "a decision will be made in due course".

At a rally, Morocco's prime minister Aziz Akhannouch also told Lekjaa: "Do not offer to host the big final game in Morocco while we still have not discussed the matter with our allies, Spain and Portugal."

"There should be some respect, brothers. Stop using electoral promises to pull the rug out from under us. These are huge matters. Deciding where the final will be held is a major issue."

Rafael Louzan, president of the Spanish football federation (RFEF), has previously said the final will be held in Spain, and felt their claim has been strengthened by winning the men's World Cup for the second time this summer.

"Even though no decision has been taken, I believe Spain is the place because it cannot be any other way," he told Cadena SER radio station. "As you know, we are currently world champions.

"I believe Spain's organisational capacity for major events is beyond question and that is why reality dictates that the grand final cannot and must not be held anywhere other than in Spain."

Spain beat Argentina to win this year's World Cup in July, although New Jersey was not confirmed as the host for the final until February 2024 - two years before the tournament took place.

Morocco are constructing a proposed 115,000-seat stadium, which would make it the largest football stadium in the world.

In Spain, Real Madrid's Bernabeu Stadium has recently been renovated and now holds 83,000, while the capacity at Barcelona's Spotify Camp Nou will be 105,000 once renovations there are complete.

49ers Week 1 overreactions: San Francisco is bigger Super Bowl threat than Rams, Seahawks appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The San Francisco 49ers asserted themselves as contenders in the NFC during their season opener. San Francisco dominated Los Angeles in a 27-7 victory in front of an international crowd at Melbourne Cricket Ground. The 49ers were competitive from the opening whistle and played with their hair on fire for a full 60 minutes.

San Francisco often looked like a forgotten team in the NFC West throughout the offseason. It is easy to understand why. Seattle won the Super Bowl, dismantling San Francisco in the playoffs as part of that journey. Meanwhile, the Rams went all in during the 2026 offseason on their quest to get back to the Super Bowl themselves. The Rams brought in Trent McDuffie, Myles Garrett, and Aaron Donald to upgrade their defense.

All of those narratives make the Rams and Seahawks easy teams to root for during the offseason. But it looks like the hype may have been overblown just two days into the regular season.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

San Francisco proved that they are the biggest Super Bowl threat in the NFC West after their huge win in Australia.

Coming into the season, the Rams were the team to beat in the NFL. Any team looking to make it to the Super Bowl has to be able to beat them.

San Francisco reminded LA, and the rest of the NFL, that they are a dangerous team when they are at full strength.

The 49ers got multiple important players back from injuries suffered last season. George Kittle, Fred Warner, Nick Bosa, and Dre Greenlaw all played major roles in last night's win against the Rams. Head coach Kyle Shanahan schemed up an excellent game on offense, completely neutralizing Myles Garrett while featuring San Francisco's deep bench of offensive talent. Even the defense looked incredible without Robert Saleh calling the shots.

Simply put, the 49ers showed that they can still outclass the Rams in all three phases of the game on the right day.

Make no mistake, a lot will change before these two teams play each other again in Week 14. It really is too early to get too invested in the 49ers running away with the NFC West after just one game.

But there is on clear takeaway from Week 1: the 49ers are not afraid of the Rams.

The 49ers should not be as afraid of the Seahawks either, especially after seeing how the defending champions looked in Week 1.

Seattle barely squeaked out a win against a bumbling New England team on Wednesday, almost exclusively because of their elite defense. Mike Macdonald's defense is still very dangerous in 2026, but Shanahan is uniquely equipped to attack that challenge. After all, the 49ers aced their test against the vaunted Rams defense last night.

The Sam Darnold injury also makes the Seahawks looks quite vulnerable after Week 1.

Darnold had an MRI on his hip on Thursday morning. It revealed that Darnold's hip is fully intact, suggesting that the injury itself may be muscular instead. Still, Macdonald already confirmed that Darnold will not play in Week 2. He also noted that Seattle does not yet know when Darnold will be able to return.

It is too early to tell how big of a problem this will be for the Seahawks moving forward. But it is not an overreaction to state that they are now more vulnerable than they were before Week 1.

San Francisco does not play Seattle until Week 5, so Darnold could easily be back by that time. However, Darnold will have to find his rhythm again and could still be one step behind by Week 5.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of Darnold's injury for the 49ers could simply be the Seahawks dropping a few close games. Every win and loss will be important this season given the three-horse race for the NFC West division crown.

The 49ers should feel more confident than ever headed into Week 2.

title: We found a bug where our type checker lied and crashed a real device
description: Chuks is a modern backend language that combines structured concurrency, async/await, and a high-performance HTTP runtime with high performance. Built for real-world services and game backends.
fullText:
Chuks v0.1.2 is the standard library release. v0.1.1 made the bytecode VM you develop against
and the native binary you ship agree on the language. This one makes them agree on the
standard library, module by module and call by call.

Every module is a thin Chuks wrapper over a native function implemented once for each execution
mode. A new differential suite drives all of them from api/stable.txt, the committed listing of
the public surface, and compares the two results cell by cell. A method joins the comparison the
moment it joins the surface, so coverage cannot drift behind the API.

463 API entries are now exercised directly by tests, including three areas that had none:
std/net end to end, std/host, and the C FFI. Everything the comparison turned up is fixed in
this release.

json.parse and the base64 decoders now throw on malformed input instead of returning a value
that reads as success:

The same sharpening runs through the rest of the library. crypto.hmac and crypto.pbkdf2
reject an algorithm they do not implement rather than computing with SHA-256 anyway.
buffer.toString rejects an encoding it does not implement. log.setLevel is honoured in a
compiled binary, so a production build emits exactly the levels you asked for.

The numeric read family reports a short read, so a truncated frame is caught at the read rather
than parsed as zeroes:

writeBytes honours its length argument, starts from the source’s read offset, and returns the
number of bytes copied:

upgradeToTLS takes the client TLS options, so STARTTLS can reach a server behind a private
certificate authority, which is the common case for an internal mail relay or database:

The same option bag works everywhere TLS is configured, and it takes cert and key for client
certificates and skipVerify for development. A ca that does not parse is refused with
ca: no valid certificates found rather than falling back to the public root store, so pinning a
private CA stays pinned.

Compiled HTTP servers rebind immediately. A deploy or a container restart no longer meets
bind: address already in use while the previous socket drains.

std/net is covered end to end now: TCP round trips, a real TLS handshake, mutual TLS, peer
certificate inspection, and the http Request surface including multipart uploads.

c.compile() builds a shared library in process from C sources, so binding a C library needs no
build system of your own:

std/chuksToC is the largest module in the standard library, 96 entries covering every call
shape, pointer arithmetic and every slice width, and all of it is now under test in both modes.
Failures raise a catchable error in a compiled binary exactly as they do in the VM: loading a
library that is not on disk, binding a symbol that is not exported, or calling with the wrong
arity all throw where you can handle them.

Multiplying an integer by 1.0 promotes it, and the promotion now survives optimization:

The same holds for x / 1.0, x + 0.0 and x - 0.0. Integer identities still fold, so
(a * 1) / b is integer division and stays 3.

These five were found by using the language rather than by testing it: writing packages for
Chuks Mobile, building an app with them, and making the documentation site compile every example it
prints. None of them is exotic, which is exactly why they were worth holding the release for.

A dataType can embed one it imported. Embedding is how a props type inherits a shared set of
fields, and it worked inside a single file. Across a module boundary the same line was rejected,
even though the imported type was perfectly usable as a parameter type two lines further down:

The embed resolver only knew about types declared in the file it was looking at. It now reads the
module’s imports too, aliases included, and an embed counts as using the import, so the name no
longer draws a spurious “imported but never used”. A package’s props type can inherit the fields
it means to accept instead of copying the list.

A comment on a chained call no longer breaks the next line. A fluent chain parsed. Annotate the
links, which is the natural way to write one, and the line after the first comment failed with
unexpected token '.':

An import can wrap before from. Breaking a long import inside the braces was accepted;
breaking it in the other obvious place was a syntax error:

Those last two were one bug. Semicolon insertion was firing at a newline while the parser was
still mid-construct. The rule now lives in one place and knows what can never start a statement:
a . continuing a chain, a ) or ] closing an enclosing expression, and the keyword from. A
line comment no longer makes that call on its own account, which was the whole of the first
symptom. Where a newline ended a statement before, it still does.

An imported type alias now expands inside a container. A unionType exported by one module and
used bare by another resolved correctly. Put it one level down, inside an array or a map, and it
did not:

Two calls from the same import, one accepted and one refused. Alias expansion happened when the
name was found in the local environment, and the cross-module path handed back the alias wrapper
untouched, so comparing element types never saw the union behind the name. It is not union-specific
either: any alias exported by one module and used inside a container by another went through the
same hole. It had presumably been latent since aliases and cross-module resolution met, because
nothing had yet put an imported alias inside a container.

A closure that captures a loop binding now warns. A const or var declared by a loop is one
slot, reused by every iteration, so a closure that outlives the iteration reads whatever the last
pass left there:

Every row selects the last tab. Nothing errors and the screen looks right until somebody taps it.
The warning names the binding and gives the fix, which is to pass the value as a parameter, since a
parameter is per-call rather than per-loop. It is a warning and not an error because a closure
invoked before the iteration ends is perfectly correct and the compiler cannot always tell the two
apart; five of its eight tests assert silence, including on the fix the message itself
recommends.

An array method used to erase the type of what it returned. .map on a []Node reported []any,
so every element downstream lost its type and a wrong annotation type-checked clean:

Underneath, the native backend copied the whole slice into a fresh []interface{} before it
dispatched, so the result came back as a pointer to that rather than the []T the program asked
for. Reading it back as its own type aborted at run time, on a device, while every assertion on
the VM stayed green.

Both halves are fixed. map’s element type is inferred from the callback’s return, and twelve
methods now compile to a real loop over []T instead of boxing and dispatching reflectively:
map, filter, flatMap, forEach, find, findLast, findIndex, findLastIndex, every,
some, reduce and toReversed. Over 300,000 elements, forEach and findIndex went from
40ms to under a millisecond, and map allocates once now rather than three times.

The speed-up reaches ordinary code because it no longer depends on the callback capturing nothing.
A callback that closes over a variable, a threshold to compare against or a counter to add to,
is the shape most callbacks actually have, and every one of them used to take the slow path.

Three more bugs came out of writing a test suite that consumes each result as its declared type
rather than printing it, which is what the previous tests did. Printing a collection cannot tell a
[]Node from a boxed one, so the bugs had been sitting under passing tests:

Hover and completion were reporting the old answers too: .map advertised -> []any from a
hardcoded string, and .filter on a []string showed a literal -> []element because array
receivers were never recorded for hover. Both now say what the method returns.

The standard library is published in two tiers, stable and experimental. api/stable.txt records
every exported symbol in the stable tier with its full signature, 682 entries, and it is checked
into the repository. A release gate stage compares the surface a build actually exports against
that file and fails on a removal or a changed signature. An addition passes.

If you depend on a stable symbol, a release cannot take it away from you without the gate saying
so first.

Nothing in this release requires a source change. Three behaviours are stricter, and code that
was relying on the old ones was relying on a silent failure:

upgradeToTLS gained an optional second parameter. Existing calls are unaffected.

The three fixes above only ever turn a compile error into working code, so nothing that builds
today can stop building. If you hand-listed fields to work around the embed, or moved comments off
a chain, you can put them back.

title: Rybakina sets up blockbuster Sabalenka final at US Open
description: Soon-to-be world number one Elena Rybakina will face Aryna Sabalenka in a blockbuster US Open final between the tournament's top two seeds.
fullText:
Soon-to-be world number one Elena Rybakina produced a gritty comeback against Coco Gauff to reach the US Open final, in which she will face Aryna Sabalenka in a blockbuster showdown between the tournament's top two seeds.

Rybakina is guaranteed to end Sabalenka's 99-week reign as world number one and will replace the Belarusian at the top when the rankings are updated on Monday.

But the Kazakh second seed could rub more salt in Sabalenka's wounds if she can deny the top seed a third successive US Open title in Saturday's showpiece.

Sabalenka sent a warning to her rivals as she overpowered home hope Jessica Pegula 7-5 6-2 to keep alive her bid to become the third woman in the Open era to win the New York singles title three times in a row.

Rybakina will stand in her way after she fought back to beat American fourth seed Gauff 3-6 6-4 6-4 and silence the partisan crowd.

"I took a deep breath and just told myself I needed to fight and show good tennis," Rybakina said.

The 27-year-old is chasing her third Grand Slam title after winning Wimbledon in 2022 and beating Sabalenka in January's Australian Open final.

It will be the first time the top two women's seeds have contested a US Open final since Serena Williams beat Victoria Azarenka in the 2013 showpiece.

Sabalenka has not been beaten in New York since losing the 2023 final to Gauff, but there were doubts over her title defence following a poor run-up to the tournament.

After a strong start to the season and winning the 'Sunshine Double' at Indian Wells and Miami in March, Sabalenka suffered a quarter-final defeat at Roland Garros and a fourth-round exit at Wimbledon.

However, she has found her form again, dropping just one set en route to the final.

"I was super desperate," Sabalenka said after her win over Pegula.

"It feels for me, talking about Grand Slams, like a last push of the season.

"I wanted it badly to go to the finals, and of course, I want to go all the way."

In a tense opening set, Sabalenka bristled with frustration early on as unforced errors crept into her game while Pegula settled quickly and struck the ball cleanly.

But eventually the four-time major singles winner found her rhythm and, after striking decisively at 6-5 to take the first set, she cranked up the power.

Pegula looked helpless as Sabalenka raced through the second set, with the Belarusian pounding 29 winners to her 12.

The victory meant Sabalenka broke the Open era record for the most Grand Slam hard-court finals in a row, with the 28-year-old reaching every major final on her favoured surface since the 2023 Australian Open.

For 32-year-old Pegula - the only semi-finalist without a Grand Slam title - it is yet another US Open defeat by long-time rival Sabalenka.

Sabalenka denied the third seed a maiden major in the 2024 final, while she also got the better of her in last year's semi-finals - although Pegula had won their most recent meeting in June's Berlin Open.

"I do think she probably would have beaten 99% of people," Pegula said.

"Probably the best match she's played this year."

Harrison & GB's Skupski into men's doubles final

Hewett & Reid into men's wheelchair doubles final

Listen: US Open - tennis remembers 9/11 25 years on

Rybakina's ascent to the top of the world rankings is already assured but she has made it clear that for all the prestige of being number one, winning titles is what she really cares about.

"It's just a number right now, my goal is to win the tournaments which I play," the 27-year-old said before her semi-final.

A three-set victory over Gauff showed all of Rybakina's resilience and ability to absorb a setback - coming from a set down and then being broken when serving for the match - before striking back.

But for much of the match, she was well short of her destructive best.

"I definitely need to step my game up [in the final], serve better than today, stay aggressive and really go for my shots," the two-time major winner added.

The prospect of a final between the top two seeds is tantalising enough but that it is the outgoing number one taking on her successor makes it all the more mouth-watering.

While Sabalenka holds the edge in the head-to-head with 10 wins in 17 meetings, including beating Rybakina in the semi-finals in Miami and the final at Indian Wells this year, the Kazakh came out on top when they met in January's Australian Open final.

Sabalenka led 3-0 in the deciding set in Melbourne but eventually fell to a third defeat in her past four Grand Slam finals.

Meanwhile, Rybakina's only loss in three previous major finals was to Sabalenka in Australia in 2023.

title: Why Nigel Benn can't walk away from Conor
description: Nigel Benn vowed to leave son Conor to plough his own path after he beat Chris Eubank Jr, but the retired world champion is back by his side this week as he prepares to face WBC welterweight champion Ryan Garcia.
fullText:
Nigel Benn had insisted he was stepping away from his son's career for good.

The 10,000-mile trips from Australia - where Nigel is based - were done, and Conor Benn was on his own after his grudge-match win over Chris Eubank Jr.

Yet in the build-up to Conor's WBC welterweight world title challenge against Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas, the 'Dark Destroyer' was by his son's side at the news conference and holding court at their Essex media day - as embedded as ever.

Ask Nigel why and he claims Conor "twisted my arm" into helping with one final hurdle.

"I don't know if he was lying or if he believed it himself," Conor says with a wry smile.

"He lives through me. He goes, 'son, this is my last fight, I'm done.' Then the next one it's, 'son, it's your first defence.' There'll always be something."

Perhaps neither man is ready to cut the cord.

Conor has stepped out of his 62-year-old father's shadow - not by matching the legendary ring achievements, but through the sheer turbulence of his own journey.

Navigating a career-threatening doping case, surviving the ferocious Eubank rivalry and acrimoniously splitting from long-time promoter Eddie Hearn transformed him from 'Nigel's boy' into one of British boxing's most polarising headliners.

Through those storms, Nigel has been there in the trenches.

"It's what Conor thinks and what his dad thinks - that's what it's about, not what everybody else says," Nigel Benn says.

"Everyone's not going to love my son. Everybody didn't love me. But once you get that belt around his waist, we'll go from there."

Thirty-six years ago, Nigel flew across the Atlantic as the fiery outsider, tearing through Doug DeWitt in Atlantic City to secure his first world title.

Now, Conor lands on the Las Vegas Strip chasing the exact same milestone. A victory would place the Benns alongside the likes of Floyd and Tracy Harris Patterson, Julio Cesar Chavez and Julio Cesar Chavez Jr and Leon and Cory Spinks in the lineage of father-and-son world champions.

"I've watched him religiously for 10 years put his life on the line," Nigel says. "He's just going from strength to strength, from glory to glory. I see him being victorious. I'm not actually worried whatsoever."

Yet reaching this point has required navigating a volatile road fraught with controversy.

The adverse drug test findings that wiped out two years of Conor's career cast a long shadow, fracturing public perception and leaving unanswered questions that still follow him.

He has always denied doping, a provisional suspension was lifted in November 2024, and he says he has fought throughout his career as "an advocate for clean sport".

Inside the ropes, the jury remains stubbornly out on his talent.

A laboured points victory over Regis Prograis in his last outing did little to convince purists he belongs at the sport's highest echelon.

But Conor cares little for the outside noise or winning over the boxing fraternity.

"To some people, I'll never be good enough," he says. "One day they love you, some day they hate you.

"You keep talking about what other people think, but I don't care. Winning the world title for me, it's personal. If I listen to other people, I wouldn't be where I am."

'Bottling it' - Garcia no-show for first Benn face-off

Benn does not deserve world title shot - Garcia

Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut

Garcia has walked an equally chaotic path, having served a one-year suspension after testing positive for banned substance ostarine following his win over Devin Haney in 2024.

Both men deny intentionally ever taking performance-enhancing drugs, but away from that issue their showdown is wrapped in the contradictions that define modern boxing.

It will be staged by UFC-backed Zuffa Boxing - following Conor's high-profile split from Hearn - yet featuring the traditional green-and-gold WBC belt on the line, despite Zuffa's public rhetoric about disrupting boxing's old-guard sanctioning bodies.

Social media spats between the fighters have brought plenty of heat, but Conor Benn does not compare it to the raw nature of the Eubank saga, which spilled over into face-to-face fury. An egg was even slapped across Benn's face by Eubank.

"Listen, it's not personal with Ryan. It is personal with Eubank - this ain't no comparison," Conor says.

"One person I wanted to put in hospital; the other one I don't. I just want his title and I want his number one position. I've been at world level for years and for me to claim the number one spot officially is the goal here.

"[Garcia] is like a child. It doesn't bother me. You need people like Ryan in the sport of boxing."

Garcia is proven at the top level and enters as the favourite, bringing blinding hand speed and a fight-ending left hook.

But Nigel Benn believes he has mapped out the exact antidote to Garcia's firepower. He says his son should attack Garcia using suffocating, bobbing aggression - the kind that Nigel used to blow out Iran Barkley in 1990.

"When he goes under pressure, what happens? He falls and his heart doesn't go into it," Nigel says.

"For the first time, [Conor] is actually sitting there listening. He has to be not the destroyer, he has to be the Dark Destroyer. Controlled aggression.

"Don't give him room. Roll under his punches, left hook to the body, left hook to the head. He knows what to do."

The hostile Vegas spotlight, meanwhile, evokes memories of Benn senior's ferocious 1995 battle with Gerald McClellan.

"Everybody had me to be blown out within round three. Exactly the same thing as what they do with Conor," Nigel says. "And I know he's going to prevail."

Win, lose or draw, Nigel insists this time he will walk away for good and let Conor do his own thing.

"I can walk out of that arena, go home, and be with my family, and that's it," Nigel says.

Whether Nigel finally catches that one-way flight back to Sydney is another matter.

If Conor leaves Las Vegas with the WBC belt around his waist, you would not bet against his father being back for defence number one.
