title: $10m on line at inaugural Ultimate Championship
description: The inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship begins on Friday. From the global stars competing to how it all works - here is everything you need to know.
fullText:
One trophy, no medals. Ten million dollars. A red carpet. A black infield. Noah Lyles as MC. Armand Duplantis singing before eyeing another world record.

This athletics season was set to be the first since the pandemic which did not culminate in an Olympic Games or World Championships.

To bridge that gap, the sport's governing body has devised a new competition.

Introducing: The World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

Across three days of competition in Budapest, live on the BBC from 11-13 September, the world's top athletes will compete for record prize money and a new title.

A new event pitching the best against the best, with increased financial commitments. You may be thinking: 'Haven't we been here before?'

Last year, Michael Johnson's inaugural Grand Slam Track league attempted to maintain focus on the sport following Paris 2024 while offering lucrative prize money, but ended after encountering serious financial issues.

This innovative, biennial format is bankrolled by World Athletics - and president Sebastian Coe has said he hopes to use it as an "incubator for change" which will shape the future of the sport's established World Championships.

So, how does the Ultimate Championship work, what do the athletes think, and is it needed? Here is everything you need to know.

The sport has long grappled with the issue of retaining the attention and excitement it generates at the Olympics throughout those four-year cycles.

Because of the disruption caused by the pandemic, and subsequent postponement of the Tokyo 2020 Games, each of the past five years have provided a pinnacle event which gathered the biggest stars in front of a global audience.

For many top British athletes, a 2026 season centred around a Commonwealth Games and European Championship on home soil would probably have finished at the Diamond League Final.

Coe and World Athletics have planned for three years to fill that perceived void.

"It is an attempt to just start experimenting a bit and innovating, with an event that will determine who really is the best of the best," Coe told BBC Sport.

"There's no guarantee we're going get everything right, and no guarantee that everything is going to work. In two years, we might look at a slightly different format.

"I also want to be able to put some of the things we're doing into the World Championship format. We have a responsibility to try and engage new young audiences."

World Athletics Ultimate Championship

Day one coverage: Friday, 11 September 18:00-21:00 - BBC Two, BBC iPlayer, BBC Sport website & app

The Ultimate features a condensed three-night schedule, held as three-hour sessions.

It is reserved for reigning Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, plus athletes who have qualified by world ranking.

However, a few star names who did not qualify have been granted exceptional invitations, including Great Britain's Josh Kerr and Norwegian rival Jakob Ingebrigtsen into the men's 1500m.

There will be a total of 28 finals, including straight finals in all field events and both the 1500m and the 5,000m. The 800m and shorter distances will have semi-finals.

Not every discipline has been included, however. World Athletics says those decisions were taken based on the popularity of each event and data it gathered on viewer behaviour, including sweat response and pulse rate.

As a result, long distance events such as the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, and field events such as the shot put and discus, have been left out.

World Athletics is providing "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport" with a total of $10m (£7.4m) to be won.

Each individual event winner will pocket $150,000 (£110,000) - more than double the offering at last year's World Championships - with $75,000 (£55,000) for the runner-up and $40,000 (£29,500) for third.

World Athletics has introduced several innovations for the inaugural event in an attempt to develop both the fan and athlete experience. They include:

The day before: The eve of the championship will include a red carpet entrance for athletes, with a designated media day featuring press conferences and photoshoots.

The lane draft: Athletes contesting the 200m will take part in a lane draft, selecting their preferred semi-final heat and lane in world rankings order.

No medals: Only the Ultimate champions will receive a trophy, which will be waiting for them to collect on a plinth at the end of their event.

Adapted for TV: There will be the use of augmented reality, athlete headshots, win probabilities and projected finishing positions to develop viewer experience.

Entertainment: Pole vault star Duplantis will perform the official song of the championship among the live acts, while American sprinter Lyles - ruled out by injury - will act as host. Centre-court style interviews will follow events.

Attention-grabbing look: The black infield is designed to steer focus to the ongoing action, with only the active competition areas highlighted in contrast.

Great Britain have confirmed a team of 22 athletes for the championship, including Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson.

Hodgkinson will be reunited with rivals Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol in the women's 800m, having taken European silver behind Werro in August.

Training partner Georgia Hunter Bell contests the 1500m seeking a fourth major title of 2026 following European, Commonwealth and world indoor success.

After winning a remarkable four European titles, Amy Hunt will race against global champions including Julien Alfred, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and Gabby Thomas in the 100m and 200m, while the mixed 4x100m relay is also included in the schedule.

European gold and silver medallists Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu contest the men's 100m alongside world champion Oblique Seville, while Matthew Hudson-Smith is in the 400m after his triumph in Birmingham.

Mile world record holder Kerr, world champion in 2023, is joined by 2022 world champion Jake Wightman in a stacked men's 1500m featuring Ingebrigtsen, Olympic champion Cole Hocker and world champion Isaac Nader.

Ingebrigtsen is also entered in the 5,000m, having returned from long-term injury to win European gold in that event last month.

'I'm not a robot' - Kerr responds to criticism before Ingebrigtsen reunion

Many of the sport's biggest names have voiced their support for athletics' new global event.

Pole vault world record holder Duplantis was named as the inaugural 'Ultimate Star' last summer and has collaborated on the official anthem for the championship, Gold, which he has written and performed.

"It's super exciting. I think it was time to try something new and innovate within athletics," Duplantis said.

"It's tough for athletes when we have years without a championship. I think this fills the gap perfectly, you want to have some sort of climax to build towards."

Kerr, set for a first race against rival Ingebrigtsen for two years, said the substantial increase in prize money showed how "serious" World Athletics are about the event.

However, while the 2023 world champion agrees that a global championship was needed, he accepts there is "probably going to be some confusion from the outside world about what this is".

"If that's what they're willing to put forward in prize money, it means that they're willing to put that effort into marketing and media," said Kerr.

"We're seeing progress. Obviously, $150,000 is a lot of money. It's not as much as other big sports, but they've earned that through years of pushing their marketing."

Hurdles star Karsten Warholm has voiced his concern regarding the impact on the calendar, describing this year's late-season schedule as "chaos".

"I think the Diamond League is a fantastic concept that should be cultivated. It will take a long time before people understand what an Ultimate Champion is," Warholm told Norwegian media outlet VG.

"It's pretty much the same athletes who participate but there could be two different winners at the Diamond League final and the Ultimate Championship.

"In terms of storytelling, it's going to be difficult. I don't think even athletics people are keeping up."

There is also the matter of the excluded athletes and events.

World triple jump champion Pedro Pichardo responded on social media to the decision to exclude his discipline: "I really don't understand what your problem is, and even less so making this decision without any explanation.

"This isn't track and field and it's not good for our sport."

After ending her season with victory in the Diamond League Final, world shot put champion Chase Jackson told Citius Mag: "My body is saying 'yes' but my pockets are saying 'why the hell am I not at the Ultimate?'

"How [do] you have track and field and just skip events? How does that make any sense?"

fullText:
The defense says: ‘It’s about competition, not conspiracy’

A US prosecutor described China’s Huawei as a criminal enterprise that stole from US companies to build its telecommunications empire, as ⁠the trial against the tech company kicked off in Brooklyn federal court on Wednesday.

“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Taylor Stout, a trial attorney from the US Department of Justice, said in the government’s opening statement. “For 20 years, that’s how Huawei, a massive Chinese telecommunications company, victimized American companies ⁠and abused the American financial system, all ⁠in an effort to dominate the telecommunications ​industry around the world.”

Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from five US companies, including operating system source code for internet routers from Cisco Systems and a robotic arm to test phones from T-Mobile, to gain an unfair competitive advantage and grow its business, ⁠the prosecutor told jurors.

“We’ll hear from people who caught Huawei red-handed trying to steal American tech,” Stout said, adding there was video of an employee stealing the robotic arm.

The defense painted a very different picture of the company and its success in court.

“It’s about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, ⁠not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct,” Brian Heberlig, one of a team of lawyers representing Huawei, said in his opening. “Huawei earned its success ... There was no blueprint for crime.”

Huawei is known ​for its telecommunications equipment, mobile phones and, in recent years, AI chips. It does ‌business globally but its networking gear is restricted in ‌the US and suppliers are banned from exporting US goods and technology to the company without approval from the Department of Commerce.

On Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said “the Chinese ‌government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises,” when asked about the case and the US prosecutor’s “criminal enterprise” description.

China “firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests”, the spokesperson said at a regular press conference.

The case against Huawei began in 2018 with an indictment charging the company and its chief financial officer with bank fraud and sanctions violations for allegedly misrepresenting its business in Iran to get around US sanctions and move millions of dollars through the US financial system.

In the ensuing years, it grew into a sprawling indictment that includes racketeering, a pattern of illegal activity conducted by an enterprise to generate profit.

Heberlig, defending Huawei, told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities ‌by global tech companies “but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal”.

He said the incidents involving Cisco and T-mobile were “actions by individual employees” and that ​management worked to make things right after learning of them.

The prosecutor also accused the company of keeping the nature of its work in Iran secret so it could launder US dollars through the financial system and could help the Iranian government spy on its own citizens. The defense said there was no evidence Huawei knew the dollar-clearing would violate US sanctions law.

In 2018, Huawei’s chief financial officer, ​Meng Wanzhou, was detained in Vancouver after being picked up on ​a US warrant as a part of the original indictment. She fought extradition for nearly three years before being freed to return to China ​in a diplomatic agreement between the US, China ‌and Canada.

The charges against her ​were dismissed in 2022 as part ​of a deferred prosecution agreement but admissions she made are set to be introduced as evidence at the trial, which is expected to last three months.

title: As Trump squeezes the International Criminal Court, more countries are leaving
description: As the United States ratchets up the pressure on the International Criminal Court, sanctioning two more high-ranking staff members in recent weeks, a small but growing number of the global tribunal’s ...
fullText:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — As the United States ratchets up the pressure on the International Criminal Court, sanctioning two more high-ranking staff members in recent weeks, a small but growing number of the global tribunal's member states have announced they will quit the institution.

The recent departure of Venezuela and Chad brings the number of countries to pull out of the court in the past year to five, joining Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The surge in withdrawals comes as the ICC faces hostility from Washington and a leadership crisis after ousting its own chief prosecutor.

"Five countries so far have announced plans to withdraw from the Rome Statute, and we welcome more announcements in the future," a spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told The Associated Press.

The Rome Statute established the ICC in 2002 as the court of last resort to prosecute individuals responsible for the world's most heinous atrocities: war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression. Based in The Hague, it takes on cases when nations are unable or unwilling to prosecute crimes on their own territory.

"The ICC regrets any decision to depart from the collective effort to end impunity for the most serious international crimes," the court's spokesperson Oriane Maillet told the AP.

In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. was launching a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty."

Rubio said he will pressure the court's 125 member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organizations that work with the court and ban staff from traveling to the United States. Trump's administration already has sanctioned a dozen ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court has issued for top Israeli officials over the war in Gaza and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.

The Central African country of Chad specifically cited the United States in its decision to withdraw. Its Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul said in a statement that in a phone call with a U.S. official on July 23, "the American side expressed its concerns regarding the functioning of this institution and requested that Chad reconsider" its membership.

Four days later, Chad said it would leave the ICC.

Iva Vukušić, a researcher at Utrecht University, told the AP that the U.S. campaign will lay bare just how committed countries are to the court. "Are they willing to defend it if it costs them something real?" she said.

The State Department told AP the U.S. would call upon nations that "enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella" to reject the ICC.

It's not just pressure from Trump that is sending ICC members toward the exit door.

The ruling military juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger blamed selective justice. The ICC has become an "instrument of neocolonial repression in the hands of imperialism," the trio said when they announced their departures last year.

A coup ousted Niger's democratically elected government in 2023. Since then, a military junta has abandoned longtime partners and has formed new alliances instead, including with Russia, where President Vladimir Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant linked to the war in Ukraine. Mali and Burkina Faso have undergone similar transformations.

"These countries are ruled by authoritarian leaders who want to avoid accountability for the harms they are inflicting on their own people," Mel O'Brien, an associate professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, told the AP.

Burundi similarly accused the court of focusing too much on conflicts in Africa when, in 2017, it became the first country to leave the ICC. The court had opened an investigation into the East African nation earlier that year.

Most of the court's initial investigations were into African countries, though most requested the involvement of the ICC.

South Africa and Gambia also announced in 2017 that they would leave but later changed course.

A change of government can also bring a country back into the fold. Hungary announced it would quit the court in 2025 but following the election of a new government, the country's parliament voted to stay.

The court also had an active investigation in the Philippines when then-President Rodrigo Duterte said his country would leave the ICC. In 2019 the Southeast Asian country became the second country to leave but as withdrawal from the court is not retroactive, the investigation continued.

Duterte is now in ICC detention in the Netherlands awaiting trial on charges of crimes against humanity for deadly anti-drug crackdowns he allegedly oversaw while in office. Opening statements are set for November.

An investigation into possible crimes committed by Venezuelan security forces under former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro will continue despite the country's announcement last month that it will also leave the ICC.

In a statement, the country's Foreign Minister Félix Plasencia said the court had been "instrumentalized to deepen inequalities among peoples and disregard their right to self-determination and sovereignty."

Venezuela is currently in the middle of U.S.-backed talks between the ruling party and the opposition following Maduro's capture in January by U.S. forces.

Ukraine is the court's most recent addition. The country joined in 2025 and previously had signed an agreement to give the court jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, following the outbreak of hostilities with Russia in 2014.

Joining the court was "Ukraine's way of saying that accountability for the gravest crimes cannot be optional, and that we intend to help build that system of justice," the country's ambassador to the Netherlands, Andriy Kostin, told AP.

title: Iran-backed terror group’s latest territorial grab threatens second global shipping chokepoint
description: Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen's Mocha port and advanced toward Bab el-Mandeb, threatening Red Sea shipping as Brent crude surged past $106.
fullText:
Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen's strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday and pushed toward positions overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, opening a potentially dangerous new front for global trade as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely constrained.

The advance threatens the southern gateway to the Red Sea just as Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on that route to bypass Hormuz — putting pressure on critical shipping lanes on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula and raising the risk of further disruptions to oil and commercial traffic through a key global trade choke point.

"Now you have Iran on one side of the Arabian Peninsula controlling Hormuz, and now the Houthis controlling Bab el-Mandeb on the other side of the peninsula," Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen advisor at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital. "Which basically is going to drive prices — oil prices, goods and everything else — up exponentially."

Iran-backed Terror Proxy Houthis Threaten Fresh Attacks After Yemen Airport Strike

On background, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

Yemeni government sources said Thursay the Houthis captured Mocha and reached the Hanish Islands, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces withdrew south toward Dhubab, which sits directly on the Bab el-Mandeb opposite the strategic island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and Perim would be critical to gaining a stronger hold over the strait, Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Sept. 10.

Bab el-Mandeb is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and connects the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and, farther north, the Suez Canal. It is a major artery for goods moving between Asia and Europe as well as energy shipments.

Its importance has grown dramatically during the Iran conflict.

Who Controls The Strait Of Hormuz Right Now? Here's What The Ship Traffic Actually Shows

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported Sept. 9 that crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through Bab el-Mandeb averaged 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, up from 5.4 million barrels per day in the final quarter of 2025. At the same time, flows through Hormuz plunged from 21.6 million barrels per day to just 4.9 million. The EIA attributed the increase at Bab el-Mandeb in part to Saudi Arabia rerouting crude through its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to avoid Hormuz.

Al-Omeisy said the danger extends beyond the Houthis' geographical gains. He said retreating government forces left behind military materiel that could strengthen Houthi forces on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."

Rubio AccU.S.Es Iran Of Flying Irgc Personnel Into Yemen As Houthi Threat Escalates

The seizure comes amid what conflict-monitoring organization ACLED described Sept. 9 as the most serious escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed camp since hostilities resumed in mid-July.

ACLED recorded at least 276 fatalities between Sept. 3 and 7 as clashes spread across al-Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwa, al-Jawf, al-Hudayda and Taizz, according to an analysis published Sept. 9.

Sherwan Hindreen Ali, ACLED's Middle East research manager, said fighting along the Red Sea coast had become particularly intense as both sides sought control over territory with direct strategic importance to Bab el-Mandeb.

"Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in al-Hudaydah and Taizz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia/IRG have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab el-Mandab," Ali said in an analysis.

Saudi Arabia itself has also become more deeply involved.

Expert Warns Of 'General Escalation' Of Fighting If Houthis Resume Red Sea Campaign

Ali said Saudi forces launched at least 15 strikes against the Houthis between Sept. 3 and 7, mostly around Taizz, marking the highest number of Saudi strikes since Riyadh resumed military engagement against the Houthis in July.

The Houthis responded Sept. 8 with what Ali described as their largest wave of direct attacks on Saudi territory since March 2022, launching dozens of drones and ballistic missiles toward Abha, Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait. Ali said the attacks injured 73 people.

The widening fighting is now posing an early test for a new joint defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.

Al-Omeisy said the international response allowed the Houthis to exploit divisions among their opponents.

"The Houthis are also good in exploiting divisions and delays, they move rapidly on the ground to force a status quo while the international community debates merits, responsibilities and costs of an intervention."

The escalation also raises questions about Saudi Arabia's newly signed defense agreement with Pakistan and Turkey.

Iran-backed Houthi Threat In Red Sea Could Lead To Major Us Policy Shift, Analysts Say

The agreement, signed last month in Mecca, states that an armed attack against one member will be considered an attack against all three, Reuters reported Sept. 10. But after Houthi drones and ballistic missiles struck Saudi cities and energy infrastructure this week, Pakistan said Thursday that no military response under the pact was currently being discussed.

"There is no such thing under discussion right now," Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said, according to Reuters. "When time comes [we] will act under the agreement."

The Houthis, meanwhile, have said international navigation through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remains safe, while maintaining that Saudi vessels are subject to their previously announced blockade, Reuters reported Thursday.

Al-Omeisy warned that reversing the Houthis' latest territorial gains could become increasingly difficult.

"The Houthis are really good at capturing a position, they entrench really well," he said. "They send these massive reinforcements, and then it's going to be extremely difficult to push them out of those areas."

Oil markets were already responding to the widening regional threat Thursday. Brent crude jumped more than 5% to $106.60 a barrel by late Thursday morning, while U.S. crude climbed above $100 for the first time since May, according to Reuters.

fullText:
Álex Rins is done with motorcycle racing. On the eve of the San Marino Grand Prix, the Monster Energy Yamaha rider confirmed he will leave MotoGP at the end of 2026, but ruled out a rumored move to the World Superbike Championship. Instead, Rins will step away from two-wheeled competition entirely and pursue a project on four wheels instead.

The rumors had been building at Magny-Cours, and Rins cleared them up himself during Thursday's media scrum at Misano. Discussions with Go Eleven reportedly fell through, and rather than chase a Plan B in WSBK racing, the 30-year-old Spaniard went a different direction entirely.

"I will not go to Superbike next year," Rins said. "I had two possibilities there. I really want to say thanks to them because they were quite interested in me. But I found another thing that really motivates me more." He added that he can't reveal the new project yet because negotiations are still on-going but hinted that it would be on four wheels instead of two.

"I'm really happy. For sure it was difficult to choose, because all my life in MotoGP, in this championship, many fights, many races, many wins," says Rins. "14 years, more or less. So yeah, I will stop with two wheels."

Rins didn't slam the door completely on bikes. He floated the idea of a limited return in the vein of Cal Crutchlow.

The decision closes a Grand Prix run that began in Moto3 in 2012. Rins finished runner-up in both Moto3 and Moto2 before moving to the premier class with Suzuki in 2017, where he earned five MotoGP wins and 18 podiums. A move to LCR Honda in 2023 delivered a victory in his third race at the Americas GP before a serious Mugello leg injury wrecked his season. His three years with Yamaha have coincided with the M1's decline; he currently sits 20th in the 2026 championship standings.

With Rins out and Fabio Quartararo bound for Honda, Yamaha will line up Jorge Martín and Ai Ogura in 2027.

description: Ryan Garcia says Conor Benn is nothing more than an "average fighter" and does not deserve a shot at his WBC welterweight title.
fullText:
Ryan Garcia says Conor Benn is nothing more than an "average fighter" and that the Briton does not deserve a shot at his WBC welterweight title.

Garcia, 28, makes the first defence of his belt against Benn at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday.

The American has consistently dismissed Benn's ability during the build-up and, after skipping Tuesday's face-off, has been accused overlooking the 29-year-old.

But Garcia says he is not taking anything lightly as he aims for a 26th win in 29 bouts as a professional.

Asked whether Benn, who has not fought at welterweight since April 2022, deserves the opportunity to challenge for a world title, Garcia said: "Not at all."

He told BBC Sport: "He's an average fighter, he's athletic and it's his last name. It's not a shot at him; it's just the bitter truth.

"I'm preparing like he's the best fighter in the world. It's all about preparation and how sharp you are.

"People could say you're overlooking him. No, I'm calling it how I see it.

"Do you want me to say he's as good as Floyd Mayweather? He's not.

"He's alright. He comes forward and throws looping overhands. He's aggressive and will make him a rugged fight, but it's not something I haven't seen before."

Garcia and Benn have documented their fight camps on social media, but have presented their preparations in different ways.

Benn has posted videos of his training regime, while Garcia has been collaborating with influencers and making appearances in the WWE.

"He's not my cup of tea. I wouldn't want to hang out with him too much," Garcia said.

"He's a bit of a hypocrite and contradicts himself a lot. I am who I am - goofy and outgoing, making jokes and having fun.

"He is trying to say he's humble, but he's out here any chance in a Rolls Royce. He loves the lights.

title: Ireland joining elite only a matter of time - Wafer
description: Aoife Wafer says Ireland are capable of joining the world's elite teams as they build on progress made in recent years.
fullText:
Back row Aoife Wafer has predicted it is "only a matter of time" before Ireland join the ranks of the very best teams in the world.

The number eight was speaking as the Irish squad prepare for a WXV campaign in which they will face the United States in Dublin on 20 September, and then Japan twice on home soil, before travelling for two Tests with South Africa in late October.

Ireland were narrowly edged out by France at the quarter-final stage of last year's World Cup and have finished third behind England and the French in the past two Women's Six Nations championships.

Scott Bemand's side won all three of their home games in the 2026 Six Nations, with Wafer scoring five tries in their five games and being named as player of the championship for a second consecutive year.

"We are bridging that gap [to the world's top teams] and it's only a matter of time before we break into that," Wafer told BBC Sport NI's Nicola McCarthy.

"We're chasing those five wins [in WXV], which is the bare minimum for us. We speak about bringing Ireland back to being one of the best in the world, being a successful Ireland, everyone is hungry to do that.

"For us it's winning those games on our home shores, making Ireland a fortress and back that up away. It's great doing it at home but why not do it away too."

The Harlequins forward endured an injury-hit 2025, missing the start of the Rugby World Cup after knee surgery and then sustaining a broken collarbone and re-rupturing her MCL.

Wafer also broke the knuckle in her right hand in the win over Scotland at the Aviva Stadium in May of this year.

"I've been working in London and trying to get the body in a good space again. I'm feeling good and ready to get back into camp and into games," said the 23-year-old.

"WXV pits the top 10 all against each other so we are fortunate enough to play Japan, USA and South Africa.

"It's a really exciting fixture coming up against USA in Tallaght, somewhere we have never played before, and then Japan, and then head to South Africa for a little bit, which will be amazing.

"We have never toured there so it'll be pretty cool. The Tests that are coming up, each of them will pose a different challenge.

"It's great to be playing five Tests and each year we seem to be playing more games. Everyone's desperate to put on an Ireland jersey, so when you can do it an extra few times a year it's even better."

Wafer highlighted some of the specific strengths of the three teams Ireland will face over the coming months.

"The USA have a bit of everything in terms of physicality, breakdown pressure, decent in the lineout, as well as some really good scrummagers, so it will be a lot for us to tackle but a really exciting opportunity too.

"The Japanese are incredible around the breakdown too, really hard to move and really rapid in the backs too.

"The South Africans are renowned for their physicality. They have a pack that will happily beat you up and backs that can also beat you up."

title: Washington Spirit sign Luvanga - but is it a record deal?
description: Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined Washington Spirit from Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football - and possibly one that sets a world record.
fullText:
Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined the Washington Spirit from Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football.

The fee paid by the National Women's Soccer League side has not been officially disclosed.

Some are reporting it to be $2.3m, external (about £1.7m), which would make Luvanga the most expensive female footballer in history.

BBC Sport has not been able to verify this figure, although a well-placed source said they believed it ranked in the top five most expensive signings in the women's game.

The Spirit declined to comment on the fee involved when contacted by BBC Sport.

Luvanga, 21, has signed a contract running to the end of the 2029 NWSL season.

If the reported record figure is correct, it would mean the fee passes the £1.4m that London City Lionesses are said to have paid to Paris St-Germain for Grace Geyoro last year.

However, the Geyoro fee has been disputed, further illustrating how transfer figures in the women's game are often kept private.

With her move, Luvanga becomes the first Tanzanian player in NWSL history.

Luvanga won the Saudi Women's Premier League in all three of her seasons with Al-Nassr, as well as the Saudi Women's Cup, Saudi Women's Super Cup and West Asian Football Federation (WAFF) Women's Clubs Championship.

She also claimed the league's golden boot last season after scoring 24 goals in 14 appearances.

The Washington Spirit are owned by Michele Kang, who also owns London City Lionesses.

London City made a series of high-profile signings during the summer transfer window, including two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas who arrived from Barcelona on a three-year deal.

Luvanga made her senior international debut for Tanzania in 2024. Before joining Al-Nassr in 2023, she played for DUX Logrono in Spain, having developed through the youth system at Tanzanian club Yanga Princess.

When discussing her new club, Luvanga said: "I am very excited to join the Washington Spirit and to take on this new challenge in the NWSL.

"I know I am arriving with the season already under way, but I'm really excited to play in a new league and a new country."

Spirit sporting director James Hocken said: "Clara adds an exciting new dimension to our attack as we head toward the play-offs.

"Despite her young age, she has demonstrated the ability to score goals in different ways and has the profile to be very successful in this league."

Luvanga's rise from Tanzania to one of the world's most competitive women's football leagues has been remarkably rapid.

She began her career with Yanga Princess in her native country before her big international breakthrough came in August 2023, when she joined Spanish side DUX Logrono. But Spain was only a brief stop on her career journey.

Over three seasons in the Middle East, she helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Women's Premier League title each time, establishing herself as one of the division's most prolific forwards.

Her time at Al-Nassr also provided an opportunity to meet one of football's biggest stars, Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr's men's team. Luvanga has spoken about modelling aspects of her own career on the Portuguese forward.

"The focus and determination that he has, when you look at his life, I wish to live like that," she told BBC Sport Africa in 2025.

There is another side to the Tanzanian forward that goes beyond the goals.

Her former team-mate at Al-Nassr, goalkeeper Sara Khalid Al-Dossary, described Luvanga to BBC Sport Africa as a great player and colleague but also revealed another of her talents: she is a great dancer.

Now Luvanga is taking both her football and her personality to the United States.

Her move to the Washington Spirit makes her the first Tanzanian woman to play in the NWSL, another significant milestone in the internationalisation of Tanzanian women's football.

She will also enter a dressing room containing a sizeable African contingent, with the Washington Spirit's roster now featuring seven African internationals.

For all her success at club level, Luvanga has not enjoyed the same impact in Tanzania colours at senior international level. Her 12 goals for Tanzania have come at youth level — 10 for the U-17 side and two for the U-20 team, while fitness problems have limited her involvement around the past two Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaigns.

Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X

Elon Musk has issued an angry tirade at the film-maker behind a four-hour documentary about his life and influence, labelling the director Alex Gibney a “bitter old man” who has “zero integrity”.

Gibney, who has previously made films about the collapse of Enron, WikiLeaks and Vladimir Putin, premiered his Musk documentary at the Venice film festival this week. He said he believed the world’s richest man was “extremely dangerous”.

In a series of posts on X, which Musk bought for $44bn in 2022, the tech mogul railed against the film as a “hit piece that misses”, adding its four-hour length also made the documentary, which is highly critical of Musk, “as boring af”.

Musk also appeared to push at conspiracy theory, reposting an image depicting the Democratic party as a puppet, controlling another puppet labelled “Team Soros” – a reference to the billionaire George Soros, who has supported progressive causes.

That puppet in turn controls another labelled “Alex Gibney”, while the Gibney puppet controls another labelled “Hollywood”. In response to the picture, Musk stated: “Accurate.”

In response to a supporter who said he had never heard of Gibney until his Musk film, Musk replied: “It’s a psy op” – a reference to a planned “psychological operation” designed to influence the public’s thoughts.

“Gibney has zero integrity. Zero,” said Musk. “Fortunately, his movies are boring af … It’s a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours.

“Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind) … He’s a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago.

“Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.”

The documentary has caused stirs since its premier, as have the claims made by some of those involved in the film.

Musk specifically denied a claim made by his ex-partner, the former Maga influencer Ashley St Clair, that his team offered her $40m to sign a non-disclosure agreement about their time together. “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims,” he wrote.

Musk also amplified a post by the podcaster Katie Miller, the wife of Donald Trump’s powerful adviser Stephen Miller and former communications director for Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. Miller complained about the alleged absence of Musk acquaintances and allies in the film.

“It simply can’t be ‘definitive’ if the people who were present didn’t participate,” she said. “This fictional movie is a hit job by a self-obsessed Hollywood director.”

Musk’s influence on public discourse through X, and the content it prioritises, is having international ripples. While he has repeatedly intervened in the immigration debate in the UK, he also celebrated the strong result for Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland in this week’s state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.

Speaking at a press conference in Venice, Gibney said he had encountered a “sense of fear” among people he approached over his film. He surmised that Musk’s childhood in South Africa may account for how he behaves now.

“He had a childhood that was very difficult and traumatic,” Gibney said. “To some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us, if I were to psychoanalyse the situation.”

Team GB return after pregnancy 'hard to put into words' - Kinsella
description: A year after giving birth, Alice Kinsella takes the latest step on her groundbreaking return to gymnastics at an international meeting for Team GB.
fullText:
Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says "it's hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking comeback to the sport continues this weekend.

The two-time European champion became the first British artistic gymnast to resume elite competition after giving birth, when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.

Now the 25-year-old is preparing for her first competition back in Team GB colours at a senior team international against France, Switzerland, Germany and Italy at Fenton Manor in Stoke on 12-13 September.

"It's kind of crazy - it's such a surreal feeling but I am very excited," Kinsella told BBC Radio Stoke.

"It's only been a year, postpartum. Training-wise, it's been tough, but it's been good. I'm excited to finally get out there. I'm ready, I'm doing everything I can to get back where I was.

"It's been a rollercoaster but a good one."

Kinsella's pioneering journey back to the sport is so rare it became the subject of a university research paper into elite gymnasts resuming their careers after giving birth.

Her son Parker, who was born in September 2025, is already a source of inspiration and he will be watching his mum compete at the weekend as Kinsella competes in all four pieces of apparatus - balance beam, bars, vault and floor - for the first time.

"It's really special because I've wanted to try to get back into a team and this is a really good start because it's a little four-way," Kinsella, who trains with Park Wrekin Gymnastics Club in Shropshire, said.

"It's not too big of a competition which is really good. I'm definitely nervous, but it's hard to put into words - it's been so long.

"I did the British [Championships] in March but only did beam and that's all I was training really but now I'm trying to do all four so it's more on the body.

"It's not like you've done one piece and you can stop thinking about everything, you've got to move on to the next and think about that. So it's been tough."

Pioneering gymnast targets rare return to elite competition after baby

'For my boy' - Kinsella makes GB gymnastics history

Gymnastics now more a mental challenge - Kinsella

After revealing she only took "three or four weeks off" after giving birth, Kinsella returned to training at the start of the year with the longer-term intention of being at the World Championships in China in 2027 and the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.

But, after finding herself ahead of schedule so far this year, she wanted to take the chance to step it up.

"My main goal was to try to get back next year but I'm actually a lot further forward than I thought I would be," added Kinsella, who won bronze in the team event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020.

"So that's why I'm doing this competition because I just want to get out there, compete, because I don't like doing nothing."

What makes Kinsella's return so unique are the obvious challenges - and changes to the body - pregnancy and childbirth brings.

There are many examples of women returning to the top of their sports after becoming mothers but gymnastics, where vital pelvic floor and core strength are both weakened during pregnancy, is different.

Kinsella said her gymnastics background has played a big part in her being able to return to physical exercise so quickly but said she "didn't feel too bad" when she got back in the gym.

"I always had that goal to get back into the gym and I think when I've got a goal set I will do everything I can to achieve it," she said.

"Getting back into a leotard with how my body's changed just feels very weird but I guess that shows what my body has gone through and I try to think about it in a positive way."

Her body is not the only thing that has changed with Kinsella adding that parenthood has helped her become better at taking the pressure off herself as an athlete.

"Having a baby changes your life - I'm very patient, whereas before Parker I was not patient at all," she said.

"When I made one tiny mistake I would get so annoyed, but now if I just make like a little mistake I'm totally fine about it.

"You have to be patient with kids, they're crazy. So I've definitely changed in that aspect but style-wise and gymnastics-wise like I don't think that's changed.

"Things are harder to get back and to do but I think the more I train it'll probably feel a lot easier."

Kinsella said when she started her comeback "no one really had any idea what I was going to able to do" and wants to keep levels of expectation for her international return as realistic as possible.

For her, this weekend in Stoke is there primarily "just to enjoy it" and to "get the experience of all four pieces [of apparatus] again".

"My body's changed, I can't do the same amount of training I used to do but I'm definitely getting back to that," Kinsella said.

"We're definitely on the right track to be where I was before I had Parker. My goal was to start competing next year properly on all four.

"It's going to be really fun. Whatever happens, happens, good, bad. I'm just proud I'm able to be back out there a year postpartum."

title: Switch Six Nations fixture to USA to grow game – World Rugby
description: World Rugby would help any nation which wants to switch a Six Nations match to the United States as it continues its drive to spread the game stateside.
fullText:
World Rugby would help any nation which wants to switch a Six Nations match to the United States, as it continues its drive to spread the game stateside.

South Africa and New Zealand have sold out the 71,000-capacity M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore for Saturday's fourth and final Test in their Greatest Rivalry series.

With the men's and women's Rugby World Cups being held in the United States in 2031 and 2033 respectively, tournament organisers are keen to bring more prestige fixtures across the Atlantic.

"In terms of the match-day economics, [South Africa vs New Zealand] is like a Six Nations match," Alan Gilpin, World Rugby chief executive, told the Daily Telegraph., external

"It starts to show that [financial return] is not the barrier. So if there is the appetite to take some of these big matches in the future to the US, we can now."

The All Blacks have been at the forefront of rugby's attempts to make an imprint in a notoriously tough sports market.

Ireland memorably beat the All Blacks for the first time when the teams met in front of a capacity 60,000-strong crowd at Chicago's Soldier Field in 2016, with a 2025 rematch proving a similar commercial success.

New Zealand have also staged matches against the United States - a 104-14 victory in front of about 40,000 fans in Washington, external - and Fiji - a 47-5 win before 33,217 in San Diego - in the country over the past decade

However Gilpin believes that the history of the Six Nations and its ability to connect with expatriate fans in the United States could be a useful tool to crack America further.

"This isn't a live discussion of an Italy vs Ireland game, but why we use that as an example?" he added.

"You've got two fantastic fanbases in the US of Irish and Italian fans

"If you could take a Six Nations game to the right place, to a Boston or to a New York, where there's a lot of those fanbases, you can definitely drive the economics.

"Now, you're going to have Irish fans and Italian fans in those respective home countries saying, 'Hang on a minute, you know, we want to see our country play?'

"The counter-argument to that [is] it's still Irish and Italian fans getting the chance to watch their team, so they're just not the ones who live in Ireland and Italy on this occasion. But that's a balancing piece we've got to work through."

Wales played their home matches at London's Wembley Stadium during the 1998 and 1999 Six Nations while the Principality Stadium was being built, but such a long-haul venue switch would be unprecedented in the tournament's 143-year history.

England women's head coach John Mitchell, who led the United States' men's team earlier in his career, said he was unsure whether a stateside expansion would ultimately succeed.

"I've worked for America. I understand that geography," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"American sport is full of rivalries and I just don't think Americans adjust to new rivalries or new franchises compared to probably some of the other countries.

"Will rugby ever go big there based on its its early investment?

"I'm not sure I can answer that, but what I do know is that rugby union is a difficult challenge for large parts of America."

He was also wary of the prospect of a Red Roses' Six Nations match being staged in the United States.

"The visibility's huge here in the European market," added Mitchell.

"Let's use it because that's the way to grow the game slowly, rather than putting huge investments into something that might have potential, but not necessarily that visibility."

While World Rugby could support a stateside Six Nations game, the decision would lie with the competing teams, all of whom would be aware of the consternation that would come with transplanting a fixture thousands of miles away.

The schedule for the 2027 editions of both the men's and women's tournaments have already been set.

title: Wall Street has thrown in the towel on a quick end to the global oil shock
description: Oil analysts are raising 2027 forecasts as disrupted Middle East shipping, shrinking stockpiles, and inflation risks linger.
fullText:
Wall Street is raising its 2027 oil forecasts with a quick return to normal looking less and less likely.

The longer crude stays elevated, the more pressure builds on consumers, inflation, bonds, and stocks.

Around the time Ben Shelton was polishing off his US Open victory over Carlos Alcaraz in the wee hours of Wednesday morning, the price of oil was making some waves of its own, climbing back above $100 per barrel.

The break into triple digits was weeks in the making. After falling below $80 in early August, oil has been on a mostly uninterrupted climb higher. Any optimism traders have around an Iran-war resolution has fizzled. They're now (re)pricing for a prolonged disruption.

But while $100 is an important psychological milestone, a deeper shift is occurring across Wall Street. There's a growing recognition that the global oil shock may not fade as quickly as investors once hoped.

Perhaps the most drastic reaction to oil's latest spike came from HSBC, which lifted its 2027 Brent forecast by a whopping $20, to $85. The firm's base case is that Strait of Hormuz flows will recover only gradually, continuing the ongoing supply squeeze.

Then there's Goldman Sachs, which raised its 2027 forecast to $80, while also flagging a worst-case scenario of $120 oil where Gulf output remains suppressed.

Not to be outdone, Bank of America said continued Middle East conflict could put oil in a $95-to-$120 range, with $150 a possibility if energy infrastructure is damaged further.

Even if those forecasts remain below oil's current price, Wall Street is now treating triple-digit crude as a realistic outcome rather than a remote risk.

Three forces are combining to sustain the ongoing oil shock. First, the Strait of Hormuz — despite occasional signs of progress — is still operating well below normal capacity.

Second, the oil stockpiles being used to cushion the blow to prices are getting thinner with every delayed shipment.

And finally, while workarounds and new routes have offered relief, they haven't helped enough to avoid a full-blown supply crisis. The old normal is far from being restored, and may never be.

A prolonged stretch of $100-plus crude oil impacts consumers well beyond the gas pump (although that certainly hurts too). It also means higher prices for diesel, jet fuel, and shipping, which can eventually touch nearly everything people spend money on: groceries, deliveries, flights, and utilities, just to name a few.

Ryan Garcia says Conor Benn is nothing more than an "average fighter" and that the Briton does not deserve a shot at his WBC welterweight title.

title: Why is there an NFL game in Australia?
description: The NFL has so far played regular-season games in seven international countries but this week's trip to Australia represents a new frontier for the USA's biggest sports league.
fullText:
The NFL has so far played regular-season games in seven international countries but this week's trip to Australia represents a new frontier.

It is the NFL's first game in the Asia-Pacific region, with the USA's biggest sports league making its longest-ever road trip for the first of a record nine international games in 2026.

It will take place about 10,000 miles from the NFL's New York headquarters, in front of about 100,000 fans at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground.

That means the Los Angeles Rams will 'host' the San Francisco 49ers on a more open oval field on Friday (01:35 BST).

But when NFL commissioner Roger Goodell visited the MCG for the first time in April, he said the historic arena "speaks to you", and it says "this is the right place to be".

American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?

Live NFL games have been broadcast in Australia since 1995 and a pre-season exhibition game was held in Sydney in 1999.

Local interest has soared since 2022, though, when the NFL made the global growth of American football a strategic priority.

The league pivoted away from a potential overseas franchise to playing more games internationally. It has invested in new markets before deciding whether to take a game there, holding year-round events to build the fanbase.

Australian players Jordan Mailata (Philadelphia) and Michael Dickson (Seattle) have also captured the imagination down under, playing for the past two Super Bowl winners.

According to the league, the number of fans in Australia has nearly doubled since 2022 to 8.8 million - almost one in three of the country's entire population.

That includes those flooding to one of the world's fastest-growing sports, flag football - the non-contact version of American football.

The NFL played a big part in flag being approved for its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028 and has expanded the sport from 10 schools in Australia to more than 500.

Now it aims to help flag football secure a spot at Brisbane 2032, with NFL executive Peter O'Reilly acknowledging that is a key reason for playing in Australia.

Being a sports-mad country, Australia was always on the NFL's radar, and after testing long-distance logistics with trips to Brazil in 2024 and 2025, the league felt ready to head down under.

Sydney and Perth were in the running but Melbourne is regarded as the nation's sports capital and the MCG is the biggest stadium in the southern hemisphere.

A deal was announced in February 2025, during Super Bowl week, and while some fans expressed anger at ticket prices when they went on sale in April 2026, they sold out in minutes.

The state of Victoria is reportedly paying up to A$15m, external (£8m) for the right to host the game but expects one of the state's biggest returns. Dublin enjoyed a tenfold return on its investment to stage its first NFL game last September.

Almost 50% of the MCG tickets were bought by fans outside Victoria or overseas, so about 50,000 fans will visit Melbourne this week.

'The G' is also right next to Melbourne Park, home of tennis' Australian Open, an ideal venue for a three-day fan festival, which began with a watch party for last night's season opener.

The NFL picked this year's Super Bowl week to announce that the 49ers will be the Rams' opponents in Melbourne, which created a buzz in Australia and California.

Not only are the Rams and 49ers regular Super Bowl contenders but they are also divisional rivals in the ultra-competitive NFC West. In addition, there is heaps of hype around the Rams.

With this season's Super Bowl being held in LA, they have gone all-in to reach the big game. First they traded for defensive stars Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie, which cemented them as championship favourites.

Then three-time defensive player of the year Aaron Donald returned from retirement and although the 35-year-old has not travelled to Australia, Garrett and McDuffie will both make their Rams debut at the MCG.

Fred Warner, Nick Bosa and George Kittle are set to return from injury for the 49ers, with Mike Evans making his debut.

The game will be broadcast live on Netflix, reaching more than 200 countries, while the Jonas Brothers will perform a half-time show.

Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season

California is 17 hours behind Melbourne and the flight takes about 16 hours. The previous longest for a regular-season game was about 12 hours to Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Yet the two teams have taken a completely different approach. The 49ers arrived in Melbourne last Friday while the Rams arrived the day before the game - just as they did for last year's comfortable win at Wembley over the Jacksonville Jaguars.

The huge time difference means that the game kicks off at 10:35 on Friday in Melbourne - which is Thursday evening in the United States: 17:35 on the west coast, 20:35 on the east.

While a morning start (local time) is virtually unheard of in the NFL, it's perfectly normal for fans used to watching cricket at the MCG.

The long flights and early start have thrown each teams' regular routine out of kilter. San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan admitted he was struggling to remember what day it was.

But having the game in week one gives each team the best chance to cope with the travel demands, rather than playing it later in the season.

Kelce's last dance? Five things to look out for in new NFL season

The NFL has committed to playing one more game in Melbourne in the next three years, with the possibility of another.

What sets Australia apart from other countries hosting international games is that ball-carrying sports are the most popular down under.

All seven Australians in the NFL converted from rugby, basketball or Australian rules football, and Australia has a huge pool of similar athletes with transferable skills.

The NFL has pledged to provide flag football kits to every school in Australia and opened an academy on the Gold Coast as it aims to tap into that talent, which could produce an international pipeline of players targeting the Olympics and the NFL.

title: Instagram boss says users will be ‘overwhelmed’ with brand content in algorithm-free world
description: Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out...
fullText:
Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out plan

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Instagram’s chief executive has said users will have a worse experience in an algorithm-free world, seeing more brand-related content, and spend less time on the app.

The comments come as the Australian government plans to give users the option to opt out of algorithms, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announcing plans on Tuesday to require social media platforms to prompt users to choose between a feed of algorithm-recommended content or a reverse chronological feed of the pages users follow. Labor also plans to introduce a range of measures designed to address online harm on the sites.

In a briefing with journalists on Thursday to launch the company’s Algo Confessions series in Australia, Instagram’s chief executive, Adam Mosseri, did not comment directly on the Albanese government proposal but said Instagram had a range of algorithms in operation. Those include ranking which friends’ stories you see more often, or which users come up first in message suggestions based on interactions, as well as the algorithm that determines the content people see in their feeds.

The launch of the series in Australia is the first outside the US. It features celebrities and influencers detailing how Instagram determines what content ends up in a user’s feed, and how the user can have some control over that by adding or removing tags in their settings.

Mosseri said just a “very vocal minority” wants social media to go back to reverse chronological feeds, which he said would just incentivise people to post more.

“What ends up happening is the best way to get more reach is just to post more often and those who can afford to post the most often do and then therefore get the most reach,” he said.

“And it turns out your friends post a lot less than creators, who post a lot less than brands and companies.”

He said people would be “overwhelmed” with content from brands, and creators and friends would be drowned out.

“What happens is people become a bit less interested in the experience and they use it a lot less, which then means that there’s less reach to go around and people start to get more and more mad about the fact that their reach is going down because the overall pie gets smaller.”

He said engagement and user satisfaction goes down.

“It’s this interesting tension between what an individual might want and what happens when you actually explode that to the entire community,” he said.

“That’s not to say that ranking is perfect, it’s not, we make mistakes – one of the things that frustrates me about ranking is that we end up over-optimising for things that we can measure and undervaluing things that are more difficult to measure.”

Mosseri said Instagram’s ranking algorithm “feels like a black box” but was something Instagram was trying to give users more control over by opting out of certain topics in their recommendations.

He said in the future, Meta’s AI models could eventually allow users to talk to the app to understand why they are seeing certain types of content.

Mosseri said he did not believe the app to be the clinical definition of “addictive”.

“I don’t believe Instagram is addictive – I know that is controversial to say – I do think we often in English anyway conflate the way we colloquially use the word addicted … like ‘I’m addicted to this show and I’m binge watching it, which is not good for me’.”

He said clinically defined addictions have withdrawal symptoms, while social media does not have that effect, and “those things are different”.

Mosseri has made this claim before. Research has found some users can have an impulse to use a platform without being fully aware of it, and evidence shows frequent engagement with algorithms “alters dopamine pathways” that fosters dependency that is “analogous to substance addiction”.

In the landmark US court case centred on the addictive nature of Meta’s products, the company’s lawyer last month conceded to the court that it was “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but the company has tools to address that. Meta later settled the case for US$18bn while denying any wrongdoing.

title: Aryna Sabalenka’s Reaction to Losing World No. 1 Ranking Goes Viral
description: ESPN captured Aryna Sabalenka’s candid reaction as Elena Rybakina ended her 99-week reign atop the WTA rankings. The post Aryna Sabalenka’s Reaction to Losing World No. 1 Ranking Goes Viral appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Aryna Sabalenka heard the roar before she saw what had happened.

The top-ranked player in women's tennis was practicing on Court P1 beside Arthur Ashe Stadium when the crowd erupted Wednesday afternoon. Sabalenka walked toward the televisions at the U.S. Open practice pavilion, leaned against a fence and watched Elena Rybakina complete the victory that ended her 99-week reign at No. 1.

ESPN captured Sabalenka viewing the final points of Rybakina's 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 quarterfinal victory over Zheng Qinwen.

There was no dramatic display. Sabalenka watched quietly, appeared to offer a small, knowing smile and then returned to work.

"Nothing she could do about it," ESPN analyst Chris Evert said during the broadcast.

It was a strikingly ordinary end to an extraordinary run.

Rybakina entered the quarterfinal needing one more victory to guarantee that she would pass Sabalenka when the WTA rankings update Monday.

Sabalenka could not influence the outcome. She had already secured her semifinal place by surviving Linda Noskova in three sets Tuesday. Even winning a third consecutive U.S. Open title would not provide enough points to remain No. 1.

Rybakina will have at least 8,681 ranking points Monday, while Sabalenka can finish with no more than 8,575, even if she successfully defends her championship.

Sabalenka stopped her practice session to watch Rybakina close out the match, then resumed preparing for Jessica Pegula.

The scene offered no evidence of anger, only recognition. Sabalenka understood exactly what Rybakina's final service hold meant.

Her uninterrupted reign, which began in October 2024, was over.

Rybakina overcame a slow, tense opening set against Zheng before taking control. She finished with 20 winners and earned the decisive break at 4-all in the third set when Zheng double-faulted.

The victory sent Rybakina into her first U.S. Open semifinal and made her the 30th woman to reach No. 1 since the WTA rankings began in 1975. She is also the first player representing Kazakhstan, male or female, to occupy the top ranking.

"It's just a number right now," Rybakina said afterward, emphasizing that she remained focused on winning the tournament.

The understated response mirrored Sabalenka's reaction from across the grounds. One player had reached the summit. The other had been displaced. Both still had matches to play.

Losing No. 1 does not eliminate Sabalenka's chance to leave New York with the trophy.

The four-time major champion will face Pegula in one semifinal, while Rybakina meets 2023 U.S. Open champion Coco Gauff in the other. A Sabalenka-Rybakina final would extend a rivalry that has already shaped the season.

Rybakina defeated Sabalenka in the Australian Open final to capture her second major title. Sabalenka responded by beating her at Indian Wells and Miami.

Now Rybakina has taken the ranking Sabalenka held for nearly two years.

The ESPN cameras preserved the precise moment Sabalenka absorbed that reality. She did not linger. She turned from the television and went back to practice, still chasing the only prize available in New York that could matter more.

title: Barry Melrose, longtime ESPN analyst former Cincinnati Stingers player, dies
description: Barry Melrose, was a longtime ESPN analyst before his Parkinson's disease diagnosis. He joined the Cincinnati Stingers of the World Hockey Association in the 1976-77 season.
fullText:
Barry Melrose, the former NHL coach who starred as an ESPN hockey analyst, has died at age 70, the network reported.

Melrose had retired from his broadcasting duties in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

"I've had over 50 extraordinary years playing, coaching and analyzing the world's greatest game, hockey. It's now time to hang up my skates and focus on my health, my family, including my supportive wife Cindy, and whatever comes next," Melrose said in a statement at the time.

"I'm beyond grateful for my hockey career, and to have called ESPN home for almost 30 years. Thanks for the incredible memories and I'll now be cheering for you from the stands."

Melrose, a defenseman, played in the NHL and World Hockey Association and went into coaching after his retirement.

Melrose joined the Cincinnati Stingers of the World Hockey Association for the 1976-77 season, and played for them until the league ceased operations after the 1978-79 season.

His 178 games played ranks eighth in Stingers' history. His 343 penalties minutes is second in club history, including a single-season record of 222 in 1978-79.

After stints in the Western Hockey League and American Hockey League, he began coaching the Los Angeles Kings in 1992 and took the Wayne Gretzky-led team to the Stanley Cup Final in his first season. The Kings lost to the Montreal Canadiens in five games in that series.

He coached the Kings for another two seasons and was fired in the third season. He also briefly coached the Tampa Bay Lightning in 2008-09.

Between the coaching stints, he was a popular ESPN studio analyst noted for his observations and his trademark mullet.

"Barry was my best friend at ESPN," John Buccigross posted on X. "A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season. Chilling and fitting--the rink was Barry's home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever."

title: Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut
description: Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world-title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.
fullText:
Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.

Benn, 29, faces WBC champion Garcia at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday in the first world title fight of his 10-year professional career.

The Briton must weigh no more than 10st 7lb (67kg) when he steps on the scales in on Friday, having not made the welterweight limit for more than four years.

"It's been extremely difficult," Benn told BBC Sport.

"It feels like I've been dragged down to the pits of hell, had a fight with Satan and God brought me back to life.

"Making weight has been the hardest thing I've done. I haven't made weight for four and a half years so it's going to be hard.

"But I won't moan when I'm getting paid a fortune to headline in Vegas for a world title. I know what I signed up for."

Benn last made the welterweight limit when stopping Chris van Heerden in two rounds in April 2022.

He stepped up to 11st 6lb (73kg) for two lucrative contests with Chris Eubank Jr last year, suffering the first defeat of his professional career in April 2025 before avenging the loss on points seven months later.

Benn's appearance in pictures and videos posted on social media during fight week has prompted concern among some observers over the effects of dropping back to welterweight.

Former world champion Carl Froch and Benn's former opponent Chris Algieri are among those to have questioned whether the weight cut could leave him depleted.

It is particularly pertinent given the contrasting styles on Saturday. Benn is an aggressive, front-foot fighter who likes to apply pressure, while American Garcia, 28, possesses fast hands and is renowned for a dangerous counter left hook.

But Benn dismissed concerns over his condition.

"I'm healthy," he said, adding that he expects to rehydrate significantly and enter the ring at around 12st 7lb (80kg) - two stones heavier than the welterweight limit.

Even if he fulfils a lifelong ambition by winning a maiden world title and following in his father Nigel's footsteps, Benn intends to vacate the belt "straight away" and move back up to middleweight or potentially as high as super-middleweight.

"I love challenges and that's what life is about, otherwise it's boring," he added.

For all the difficulty presented by the weight cut, there was little outward sign of Benn being weighed down by the occasion.

He was relaxed and in good spirits as he made time for the travelling British media at the UFC's Meta Apex, with father and British boxing great Nigel Benn by his side.

The former two-weight world champion has been a prominent presence throughout fight week, despite previously suggesting he would take a step back from his son's career.

One man Conor Benn is yet to see, however, is his opponent.

Garcia did not appear for a scheduled face-off at Mandalay Bay on Tuesday, with Benn told beforehand that the champion would not be attending.

Benn turned up regardless and jokingly squared up to his 62-year-old father instead.

He described Garcia as a "strange geezer" and said the no-show had done the champion "no favours".

"I'm not bothered, I've dealt with worse," Conor Benn added. "If he turns up or not, it makes no difference to me.

"Irrespective of how hard the weight cut is or anything else, we owe it to the public to give the fans what they want. It's a lack of discipline and professionalism."

title: Gauff saves match points to set up Rybakina semi-final
description: Coco Gauff saves two match points to beat Mirra Andreeva and set up a US Open semi-final against incoming world number one Elena Rybakina.
fullText:
Coco Gauff saved two match points as she fought from a set down to beat Mirra Andreeva and set up a US Open semi-final against incoming world number one Elena Rybakina.

Blown away in a 26-minute opening set, fourth seed Gauff was twice pegged back from a break up in a scrappy second set before coming through a 16-point tie-break to force a decider.

Roared on by a partisan crowd, the American's resilience proved the difference in what became a mental battle as she closed out a 2-6 7-6 (9-7) 6-2 win – a performance she said was inspired by compatriot Frances Tiafoe's comeback victory over Alex Michelsen on Tuesday night.

Progression to the last four marks back-to-back Grand Slam semi-finals for the two-time major champion and her first in New York since winning the title in 2023.

It is the first time the top four seeds have reached the semi-finals of the women's singles at a major since Wimbledon in 2009, after top seed Sabalenka and third seed Jessica Pegula progressed on Tuesday.

"At the end of the first set I was thinking about Frances and how he came back yesterday," Gauff said.

"We all want to do well in front of this crowd. Honestly, I was just trying to leave the court with no regrets."

Gauff also drew strength from her home crowd, something she has learned to embrace having struggled with the pressure of "disappointing" them with a "bad match" earlier in her career.

"I don't have that fear of disappointing them. I'm just using them and knowing that when I step on this court, they're still going to have my back," she said.

Earlier, second seed Rybakina recovered from losing a set for the first time this tournament - and going break-point down in the decider - to beat Zheng Qinwen 3-6 6-1 6-4.

The 27-year arrived at the US Open trailing Aryna Sabalenka by just 434 points and was guaranteed to secure the number one ranking for the first time in her career by reaching the semi-finals.

'Just a number' - Rybakina's rise to world number one

Rybakina reaches #1 as Gauff completes epic semis line-up

This was an uncharacteristic performance from Gauff, whose 22 winners were vastly outnumbered by 42 unforced errors, including 12 double faults.

She won just five of the opening 21 points as Andreeva breezed into a one-set lead and later failed to consolidate breaks at 4-2 and 5-3 in the second set.

A double fault at the beginning of the tie-break felt ominous, but the 22-year-old maintained her composure to save two match points - something which proved a turning point as she dominated the clutch moments in the decider.

Her response was in stark contrast to Andreeva, who struck 14 unforced errors to Gauff's two in the final set and flung a racquet in frustration following the first break of serve.

"You have to admire how Coco does this. She's done it so many times in her career," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"She's unrecognisable from the player at the start of this match. She was subdued and playing defensive tennis. By the end, she was completely controlling the match.

"We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court.

"It's the ability of one of the gladiators to get themselves back in it."

Addressing her outburst, Andreeva said: "I felt like I was holding my emotions for too long, not reacting on a lot of points. At one point I felt like needed to let it out."

Rybakina's ascension to the top of the rankings – the first Kazakhstani man or woman to do so – will rightly dominate the headlines.

She has achieved one of her two goals for the tournament and is now just two wins away from a second major title of the season, having won the Australian Open in January.

However, beaten opponent Zheng's achievements should not go unnoticed, offering a welcome reminder of her talent with an entertaining run to the last eight.

Having dropped out of the top 100 following elbow surgery in July 2025, the reigning Olympic champion navigated three qualifying rounds before registering her first Grand Slam main-draw win since last year's French Open.

She later stunned 22nd seed Madison Keys, who she trailed 5-0 in the third set and saved match point, and eighth seed Iga Swiatek to reach her third quarter-final in New York.

Ranked 121st heading into the tournament, she is now up to 52nd in the live rankings and has just 65 points to defend for the remainder of the season.

But for all the positives, there is an unshakable sense of what might have been against Rybakina.

Momentum was with the 23-year-old after she broke late in the first set before staving off five break points to take a 1-0 lead. However, she was completely blown away in the second set, with her second serve coming under considerable pressure.

She earned a break point in the eighth game of the decider but missed a routine backhand pass. In the next game, she brilliantly fought back from 0-40 to deuce but then followed a loose backhand with a double fault as her hopes of a maiden US Open semi-final slipped away.
